# How to use this guide

Remedial Biology is for students who took mathematics instead of biology in Class 12. It assumes no biology at all: every term is explained the first time it appears, so read the units in order. Unit 1 builds the vocabulary of plants, Units 2 and 3 cover the human body, Unit 4 returns to plant nutrition, and Unit 5 ends with respiration, growth, the cell and tissues.

**Study plan.** One unit every two or three days. Read the notes once fully, then draw each text diagram from memory (heart, nephron, neuron, flower, dicot and monocot stem, chloroplast, cell). Learn the tables as tables — examiners like a neat comparison. Finally answer the question bank aloud or on paper, and take the quick MCQ test to check facts.

**Units as in the syllabus.** The five notes follow the five PCI units exactly. Units 2, 3 and 5 are long because each joins several topics (for example, Unit 3 has excretion, nerves, hormones and reproduction); they are kept together so that your notes match the syllabus copy your college gives you.

## The exam for this subject

In the PCI scheme, **BP106RBT is a Non University Examination (NUE)**: your own college sets and conducts the end-semester paper. It is a **35-mark, 1.5-hour** paper, and the subject carries 50 marks in all.

| Part | Marks |
| --- | --- |
| Continuous mode (attendance, assignments) | 5 |
| Sessional examinations (1 hour each) | 10 |
| **End-semester examination (1.5 hours)** | **35** |
| Total | 50 |

**End-semester paper (35 marks, 1.5 hours)** — the pattern the PCI regulations give for a 35-mark paper:

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | Long answers — attempt 1 of 2 | 1 × 10 = 10 |
| II | Short answers — attempt 5 of 7 | 5 × 5 = 25 |

There is **no MCQ section** in this paper. The MCQs and the quick MCQ test here are for practice and for checking facts quickly, and they help with viva and sessional questions. Because your college sets the paper, a few colleges may change the split; the full mock follows the PCI pattern.

**Sessional paper (30 marks, 1 hour), as PCI gives it for NUE subjects:** long answers 1 of 2 × 10 = 10, short answers 4 of 6 × 5 = 20. A mock in this pattern is also included.

The practical, **BP112RBP**, carries 25 marks: 10 internal and 15 in a 2-hour end-semester practical. Its guides are in the practicals section.

Your college may adjust the paper slightly; confirm the pattern with your teachers. To pass you need 50% of the total of internal and end-semester marks together.

## Probability ratings

- **High** — asked in most papers; prepare a full answer with a labelled diagram.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare; good for a backup choice and for viva questions.

These ratings are estimates from syllabus weight and common question patterns. They are not a promise of what will be asked.

## Where the marks usually come from

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Living world, plant morphology | Five-kingdom classification, binomial nomenclature, modifications of root and stem, placentation and aestivation, types of fruits, anatomy of dicot and monocot stem and root |
| 2 Blood, heart, digestion, breathing | Composition of blood, coagulation, blood groups, structure of heart and cardiac cycle, ECG, digestive enzymes, mechanism of breathing, transport of gases, respiratory volumes |
| 3 Excretion, nerves, hormones, reproduction | Nephron and urine formation, renin–angiotensin system, neuron and nerve impulse, functions of brain parts, endocrine glands and hormones, spermatogenesis and oogenesis, menstrual cycle |
| 4 Mineral nutrition, photosynthesis | Macro- and micronutrients with deficiency symptoms, nitrogen cycle, root nodule formation, light and dark reactions, factors affecting photosynthesis |
| 5 Respiration, growth, cell, tissues | Glycolysis and fermentation, phases and curve of growth, plant growth regulators, cell organelles, mitosis and meiosis, plant and animal tissues |

## Scoring tips for this subject

1. **Draw first.** A labelled diagram earns marks even before you write a word. Practise the heart, nephron, neuron, flower (longitudinal section), dicot stem section, chloroplast, mitochondrion and a plant cell.
2. **Use tables for differences.** "Differentiate" or "compare" questions (mitosis vs meiosis, dicot vs monocot stem, arteries vs veins, spermatogenesis vs oogenesis) are easiest to score as a 5–6 row table.
3. **Give examples with families** for plant topics: carrot (Apiaceae), potato (Solanaceae), pea (Fabaceae), mustard (Brassicaceae), maize (Poaceae). Write scientific names in proper binomial form.
4. **Use flow charts** for processes: coagulation, urine formation, renin–angiotensin system, glycolysis, nitrogen cycle, spermatogenesis.
5. **Learn the standard numbers:** RBC about 5 million/mm³, heart rate 72/min, cardiac cycle 0.8 s, cardiac output about 5 L/min, BP 120/80 mmHg, tidal volume 500 ml, GFR 125 ml/min (180 L/day), resting potential −70 mV, net ATP of glycolysis 2.
6. **Spell key terms correctly**: renin (kidney) vs rennin (stomach), ileum (gut) vs ilium (hip bone), mitosis vs meiosis.
7. **Link to pharmacy** in one line at the end of a long answer where you can (ACE inhibitors and the renin–angiotensin system, insulin and diabetes, fermentation for alcohol and antibiotics, vitamin K and clotting). It shows understanding.
8. In 1.5 hours you write six answers: give the long answer about 25 minutes and each of the five short answers about 12 minutes, leaving a few minutes to check labels and diagrams.

# Study of the compound microscope

**Aim:** To study the parts, working and care of a compound microscope and to use it to observe a prepared slide.

> Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ from this guide.

## Principle

A **compound microscope** magnifies an object in two stages using two lens systems. The **objective lens** (near the object) forms a real, inverted, enlarged image inside the tube. The **eyepiece (ocular)** magnifies this image again, giving a virtual, enlarged image seen by the eye.

**Total magnification = magnification of objective × magnification of eyepiece.**

**Resolving power** is the ability to show two close points as separate. It, not magnification alone, decides how much detail is seen. Using **cedar wood oil** with the oil-immersion objective improves resolution because the oil has a refractive index close to that of glass, so less light is lost by bending.

## Requirements

Compound microscope, a prepared slide (for example a stained onion peel or a T.S. of stem), lens paper (tissue), cedar wood oil, xylene (for cleaning the oil-immersion lens).

## Parts of a compound microscope

```text
               eyepiece (ocular, 5x / 10x / 15x)
                  |
               body tube
                  |
  coarse adj. - revolving nosepiece -- objectives (10x, 45x, 100x oil)
  fine adj.        |
     |          [ stage with clips ]  <- slide placed here
   arm             |
     |          condenser + iris diaphragm
     |             |
   (pillar)     mirror (plane / concave) or built-in lamp
     |
   base (foot)
```

| Part | Function |
| --- | --- |
| **Base (foot)** | Horseshoe-shaped support |
| **Pillar and arm** | Hold the body; arm is used to carry the microscope |
| **Inclination joint** | Allows tilting for comfortable viewing |
| **Stage** | Flat platform with a central hole; holds the slide with clips; mechanical stage moves it smoothly |
| **Mirror** | Reflects light upward; **plane** side for strong light, **concave** side for weak light (when no condenser) |
| **Condenser** | Focuses light onto the object |
| **Iris diaphragm** | Controls the amount of light |
| **Body tube** | Holds the eyepiece at the top and nosepiece at the bottom |
| **Revolving nosepiece** | Holds the objectives; rotated to change them |
| **Objectives** | Low power (10×), high power (40× or 45×), oil immersion (100×) |
| **Eyepiece** | Usually 10×; magnifies the image formed by the objective |
| **Coarse adjustment** | Large knob; moves the tube or stage quickly for rough focus |
| **Fine adjustment** | Small knob; slow movement for sharp focus, especially at high power |

## Procedure

1. Carry the microscope with one hand on the arm and the other under the base; place it on the bench with the arm towards you.
2. Clean the lenses gently with lens paper only.
3. Bring the low-power (10×) objective in line with the tube (it clicks into place).
4. Look through the eyepiece and adjust the mirror (or lamp) and diaphragm until the field is evenly bright.
5. Place the slide on the stage, with the object over the hole, and fix it with clips.
6. Looking from the side, lower the objective with the coarse knob until it is about 0.5 cm above the slide (never let it touch).
7. Looking through the eyepiece, raise the objective slowly with the coarse knob until the object comes into view; sharpen with the fine knob.
8. Move the area of interest to the centre, then rotate the nosepiece to the high-power objective; refocus only with the fine knob.
9. For oil immersion: put a drop of cedar wood oil on the slide, swing in the 100× objective so it dips into the oil, and focus with the fine knob. Afterwards wipe the lens with lens paper moistened with a little xylene.
10. Draw what you see and note the magnification used.

## Observations

| Objective | Eyepiece | Total magnification | What was seen |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10× | 10× | 100× | Outline of cells |
| 45× | 10× | 450× | Cell wall, nucleus |
| 100× (oil) | 10× | 1,000× | Fine detail |

## Result

The parts of the compound microscope were studied and a prepared slide was focused at low power, high power and (where available) oil immersion.

## Precautions

1. Never focus downward with the coarse knob while looking through the eyepiece; the lens may hit and break the slide.
2. Use only the fine adjustment at high power.
3. Clean lenses only with lens paper; never touch them with fingers.
4. Remove oil from the oil-immersion lens after use.
5. Keep the microscope covered and dry after use, with the low-power objective in place.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the total magnification with a 10× eyepiece and a 45× objective?** 450×.
2. **Why is cedar wood oil used with the 100× objective?** Its refractive index is close to glass, so light is not lost by bending and resolution improves.
3. **When is the concave mirror used?** In weak light, when there is no condenser.
4. **What is resolving power?** The ability to show two close points as separate.
5. **Which knob is used at high power?** The fine adjustment only.
6. **What kind of image does a compound microscope form?** Virtual, inverted and magnified.

# Section cutting techniques (free-hand sections)

**Aim:** To cut thin free-hand transverse sections (T.S.) of a stem, root or leaf for microscopic study.

> Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ from this guide.

## Principle

Plant organs are too thick for light to pass through, so the internal structure (anatomy) can only be seen in very thin slices called **sections**. A **transverse section (T.S.)** is cut at right angles to the long axis; a **longitudinal section (L.S.)** is cut along it. A section one or two cell layers thick lets light pass and shows each tissue clearly. In the free-hand method a sharp razor is drawn across the material by hand; soft material is supported in a **pith** block (potato, carrot or elder pith) so that it does not bend.

## Requirements

Fresh material (sunflower or *Cucurbita* stem, maize stem, gram or maize root, or a leaf), sharp razor, watch glass with water, fine brush, potato or carrot piece (as pith), needle, forceps, slides, coverslips, glycerine, microscope.

## Procedure

1. Take a straight piece of the stem or root about 2–3 cm long. A thin leaf or slender root is held between two halves of a potato or carrot block slit lengthwise.
2. Hold the material vertically between the thumb and forefinger of the left hand, with its top a little above the fingers.
3. Make the top surface flat with one cut and discard that slice.
4. Wet the razor blade and the material with water.
5. Hold the razor in the right hand, blade horizontal and at right angles to the material, edge facing you.
6. Draw the razor quickly across the top of the material in one smooth stroke, from the heel of the blade to its tip (pulling towards yourself). Do not saw back and forth.
7. Cut many sections in quick succession, keeping material and razor wet.
8. Transfer the sections from the blade to the watch glass of water with a wet brush.
9. Select the thinnest, complete, uniform sections (they look transparent) using a brush.
10. Place one on a slide in a drop of water or glycerine; stain and mount it (see the mounting and staining practical) and observe.

```text
         razor (horizontal, wet)
     ===========================>  one smooth pull
        | material |
        |  held    |   thumb and forefinger hold it upright
        | between  |
        | fingers  |
```

## Observations

Draw the section seen at low power and label the tissues (epidermis, cortex, endodermis, pericycle, vascular bundles, pith). Record the identifying features, for example "vascular bundles in a ring, open → dicot stem".

| Section | Key features seen | Identified as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 |  |  |
| 2 |  |  |

## Result

Thin, uniform transverse sections of ______ were cut free-hand and observed under the microscope.

## Precautions

1. Use a very sharp razor; a blunt one crushes the cells.
2. Keep the material and razor wet to avoid drying and air bubbles.
3. Cut in one smooth stroke; keep the blade at right angles to the material for a true transverse section.
4. Handle sections with a brush, not with forceps or fingers.
5. Choose thin, complete sections; thick ones look dark.
6. Handle the razor carefully to avoid cuts.

## Viva questions

1. **Why must sections be thin?** So light can pass through and individual cells and tissues are seen.
2. **What is a T.S.?** A section cut at right angles to the long axis of the organ.
3. **Why is pith (potato) used?** To support soft or thin material while cutting.
4. **Why keep the razor wet?** To prevent drying of sections and to let them slide off easily.
5. **How do you pick a good section?** It is thin, transparent, complete and of even thickness.
6. **Name a tissue you can identify in a dicot stem T.S.** Collenchymatous hypodermis, a ring of open vascular bundles, or pith.
practicals.title: Section cutting techniques (free-hand sections)

# Mounting and staining of sections

**Aim:** To stain a plant section (single or double staining) and mount it on a slide for microscopic study.

> Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ from this guide. Dilute HCl and alcohol are irritant and flammable; handle with care.

## Principle

Most plant cells are colourless, so tissues are hard to tell apart. **Stains** are dyes that colour particular parts. For example:

| Stain | Colours | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Safranin** (red) | Lignified walls (xylem, sclerenchyma) and nuclei red | Lignified tissue |
| **Fast green** or light green | Cellulose walls (parenchyma, phloem) green | Unlignified tissue |
| **Phloroglucinol + concentrated HCl** | Lignified walls pink-red | Test for lignin |
| **Iodine solution** | Starch blue-black; proteins yellow | Cell inclusions |
| **Acetocarmine** or methylene blue | Nuclei | Cells, onion peel, cheek cells |

Using two stains (**double staining**, e.g. safranin and fast green) gives contrast: lignified tissues red, cellulose tissues green.

**Mounting** means placing the material in a liquid (**mountant**) under a coverslip. Water or **glycerine** is used for temporary mounts; glycerine does not dry quickly and makes tissue clearer. **DPX** or Canada balsam is used for permanent mounts.

## Requirements

Thin sections (from the section cutting practical), watch glasses, brush, needle, safranin, fast green, phloroglucinol, concentrated HCl, glycerine, slides, coverslips, blotting paper, microscope.

## Procedure

**A. Single staining (safranin) — temporary mount**

1. Place a few good sections in a watch glass of water.
2. Transfer them to a watch glass of dilute safranin for 2–5 minutes.
3. Wash in water to remove extra stain until the water runs clear.
4. Put a drop of glycerine at the centre of a clean slide and place one section in it with a brush.
5. Lower the coverslip slowly at an angle using a needle so that no air bubbles are trapped.
6. Remove extra glycerine from the edges with blotting paper.
7. Observe under low power, then high power.

**B. Double staining (safranin and fast green) — temporary**

1. Stain with safranin and wash as above.
2. Dip in fast green for a few seconds only (it stains quickly).
3. Wash, mount in glycerine and observe: lignified xylem red, parenchyma and phloem green.

**C. Lignin test (phloroglucinol and HCl)**

1. Put a section on a slide; add a drop of phloroglucinol, wait a minute, then add a drop of concentrated HCl.
2. Cover and observe: lignified walls (xylem, sclerenchyma) turn pink-red.

```text
  coverslip lowered at an angle with a needle
        \
         \______
  =======[ drop + section ]=======  slide
```

## Observations

| Tissue | Colour with safranin | Colour with fast green | Phloroglucinol/HCl |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Xylem | Red | — | Pink-red |
| Sclerenchyma | Red | — | Pink-red |
| Parenchyma (cortex, pith) | Light / unstained | Green | No colour |
| Phloem | Light | Green | No colour |

## Result

The section was stained with ______ and mounted in glycerine; lignified tissues were stained ______ and cellulose tissues ______.

## Precautions

1. Do not overstain; wash out excess stain.
2. Fast green acts quickly; keep its time short.
3. Lower the coverslip slowly to avoid air bubbles.
4. Keep the slide and coverslip clean and dry outside the mount.
5. Use only one section per mount, at the centre of the slide.
6. Add concentrated HCl carefully; it is corrosive.

## Viva questions

1. **Why are sections stained?** To colour different tissues so they can be distinguished.
2. **What does safranin stain?** Lignified walls and nuclei red.
3. **What is double staining?** Using two contrasting stains, such as safranin and fast green, on the same section.
4. **Why is glycerine used as a mountant?** It does not dry quickly and clears the tissue.
5. **How do you avoid air bubbles?** Lower the coverslip slowly at an angle with a needle.
6. **What is the test for lignin?** Phloroglucinol with concentrated HCl gives a pink-red colour.
practicals.title: Mounting and staining of sections

# Permanent slide preparation

**Aim:** To prepare a permanent, double-stained slide of a plant section (for example T.S. of a dicot stem).

> Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ from this guide. Alcohol and xylene are flammable; work away from flames in a ventilated area.

## Principle

A temporary mount in water or glycerine dries out or decays in days. A **permanent slide** lasts for years. To make one, the section is:

1. **Stained** (safranin for lignified tissue, fast green for cellulose tissue).
2. **Dehydrated** — all water is removed gradually through a series of increasing alcohol strengths (30% → 50% → 70% → 90% → absolute alcohol). Sudden transfer would shrink and distort the cells, so the change is made in steps.
3. **Cleared** — placed in **xylene** (or clove oil), which makes the tissue transparent and is miscible with the mountant. Water left behind makes the section milky in xylene.
4. **Mounted** in a resinous medium such as **DPX** or **Canada balsam**, which hardens and seals the coverslip.

## Requirements

Thin sections, watch glasses, brush, safranin (in 50% alcohol or water), fast green (in alcohol or clove oil), alcohol grades 30%, 50%, 70%, 90% and absolute alcohol, xylene, DPX or Canada balsam, slides, coverslips, labels, slide tray.

## Procedure

```text
 Water -> safranin (5 min) -> wash
   -> 30% -> 50% -> 70% alcohol (about 2 min each)
   -> 90% alcohol -> fast green (a few seconds)
   -> absolute alcohol (2 changes)
   -> xylene (clearing)
   -> mount in DPX / Canada balsam -> label -> dry flat
```

1. Select thin, complete sections and place them in water.
2. Stain in safranin for about 5 minutes; wash off extra stain.
3. Pass through 30%, 50% and 70% alcohol, about 2 minutes each.
4. Transfer to 90% alcohol, then dip in fast green for a few seconds.
5. Transfer to absolute alcohol, two changes, to complete dehydration.
6. Clear in xylene for a few minutes. If the section looks milky, water is still present: return it to absolute alcohol and repeat.
7. Place a drop of DPX or Canada balsam at the centre of a clean slide, put the section in it, and lower the coverslip slowly at an angle.
8. Label the slide (name of specimen, stain, date) and keep it flat to dry.
9. Observe under the microscope after drying.

## Observations

Draw the section and label tissues. Note the colours: lignified xylem and sclerenchyma red; parenchyma, phloem and collenchyma green.

## Result

A permanent double-stained slide of ______ was prepared.

## Precautions

1. Dehydrate gradually; skipping grades distorts cells.
2. Dehydration must be complete before xylene, or the section turns milky.
3. Fast green stains quickly; keep the time short.
4. Avoid air bubbles under the coverslip.
5. Keep xylene and alcohol away from flames; use gloves.
6. Store the slide flat until the mountant hardens.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is dehydration done through grades of alcohol?** Sudden removal of water shrinks and distorts the cells.
2. **What is clearing?** Making the tissue transparent with xylene or clove oil, which also mixes with the mountant.
3. **Why does a section turn milky in xylene?** Water is still present (incomplete dehydration).
4. **Name two permanent mountants.** DPX and Canada balsam.
5. **Difference between temporary and permanent slides?** Temporary (water or glycerine) lasts a short time; permanent (dehydrated, cleared, mounted in resin) lasts for years.
6. **Why label a slide?** To record specimen, stain and date for later identification.
practicals.title: Permanent slide preparation

# Study of the cell and its inclusions

**Aim:** To study the structure of plant and animal cells (onion peel and human cheek cells) and to identify cell inclusions such as starch grains, aleurone grains and calcium oxalate crystals.

> Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ from this guide. Use a new, sterile toothpick or spatula for cheek cells and discard it safely.

## Principle

A **cell** is the basic unit of life. Plant cells have a cellulose **cell wall**, a large **vacuole** and (in green parts) chloroplasts; animal cells have only a **cell membrane**. Stains make parts visible: iodine or safranin for onion peel, methylene blue for cheek cells.

**Cell inclusions** are non-living substances stored in cells: food reserves and waste products. Identifying them is important in pharmacognosy, where powdered drugs are recognised by their starch grains and crystals.

| Inclusion | Test or appearance | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Starch grains** | Blue-black with iodine; show a **hilum** (point) and concentric layers (**striations**) | Potato (eccentric hilum), rice (small polygonal), maize, wheat |
| **Aleurone grains** (protein) | Yellow to brown with iodine | Castor seed, aleurone layer of maize |
| **Calcium oxalate crystals** | Insoluble in acetic acid, soluble in HCl without effervescence; seen as prisms, needles (**raphides**), clusters (**rosettes**) | Raphides in *Colocasia*; prisms and rosettes in many leaves and barks |
| **Calcium carbonate (cystoliths)** | Dissolve in acid with effervescence (bubbles of CO2) | *Ficus* leaf |
| **Oil globules** | Red with Sudan III | Oil seeds |

## Requirements

Onion bulb, potato tuber, rice or maize grains, castor seeds, *Colocasia* petiole; iodine solution, safranin, methylene blue, 0.9% saline, acetic acid, dilute HCl, glycerine, Sudan III; slides, coverslips, forceps, needles, blade, sterile toothpick, microscope.

## Procedure

**A. Onion peel (plant cell)**

1. Remove a fleshy scale leaf from an onion and peel off the thin inner epidermis with forceps.
2. Place it in water on a slide; add a drop of iodine or safranin for 1–2 minutes; wash.
3. Mount in glycerine, cover and observe.

**B. Cheek cells (animal cell)**

1. Rinse your mouth; gently scrape the inside of the cheek with a sterile toothpick.
2. Spread the scraping in a drop of saline on a slide; add a drop of methylene blue; wait a minute, blot extra stain.
3. Cover and observe.

**C. Inclusions**

1. Scrape a little cut potato surface onto a slide with water; add iodine; observe starch grains.
2. Crush a little castor endosperm in water; add iodine; observe aleurone grains.
3. Scrape *Colocasia* petiole tissue in water; observe needle-shaped raphides; add acetic acid (no change) and then HCl (crystals dissolve without bubbles).

## Observations

| Specimen | Features seen |
| --- | --- |
| Onion peel | Rectangular cells in rows, cell wall, nucleus at one side, large vacuole, no chloroplasts (scale leaf is not green) |
| Cheek cells | Flat, irregular cells, thin membrane, central nucleus stained blue, no wall, no large vacuole |
| Potato starch | Oval grains, eccentric hilum, striations, blue-black with iodine |
| Castor aleurone | Yellow-brown protein grains with iodine |
| *Colocasia* | Bundles of needle-shaped raphides of calcium oxalate |

Draw each and label.

## Result

Plant and animal cells were observed and compared, and the cell inclusions ______ were identified.

## Precautions

1. Take a thin, single-layer peel; avoid folding.
2. Do not overstain.
3. Use sterile, disposable toothpicks; never reuse them.
4. Lower the coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles.
5. Use small amounts of iodine; too much masks details.

## Viva questions

1. **Name two differences between onion and cheek cells.** Onion has a cell wall and a large vacuole; cheek cells have neither.
2. **Why is the onion peel colourless?** The scale leaf grows underground and has no chloroplasts.
3. **How is starch identified?** It turns blue-black with iodine.
4. **What is a hilum of a starch grain?** The point around which layers of starch are deposited.
5. **What are raphides?** Needle-shaped crystals of calcium oxalate, as in *Colocasia*.
6. **How do you tell calcium carbonate from calcium oxalate?** Carbonate dissolves in acid with effervescence; oxalate dissolves in HCl without bubbles and does not dissolve in acetic acid.

# Study of stem, root, leaf, seed, fruit, flower and their modifications

**Aim:** To study the external features (morphology) of root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit and seed of flowering plants, and to identify their modifications with examples and families.

> Specimens vary with season and region; use whatever your laboratory provides. Follow your lab manual and your teacher.

## Principle

**Morphology** is the study of external form. Each plant part has a basic plan, but many are **modified** (changed in form) to do extra jobs such as storage, support, climbing or protection. A specimen is identified by looking for the basic features that remain: a stem has nodes, internodes and buds; a root has no nodes or buds; a leaf arises at a node and has a bud in its axil.

## Requirements

Fresh or preserved specimens (listed below), hand lens, forceps, needle, blade, notebook.

## Procedure

1. Observe each specimen with the naked eye and a hand lens.
2. Note the basic features that show which organ it is (nodes, buds, scale leaves, root hairs).
3. Identify the modification and its function.
4. Cut flowers, fruits and seeds where needed (L.S. of flower, T.S. of ovary, opened seed).
5. Draw a labelled diagram and write the identifying features.

## Specimens and identifying features

**Roots**

| Specimen (family) | Modification | Identifying features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Carrot (Apiaceae) | Conical storage root | Swollen tap root tapering downward; no nodes or buds |
| Radish (Brassicaceae) | Fusiform | Swollen in the middle, tapering at both ends |
| Turnip (Brassicaceae), beetroot (Amaranthaceae) | Napiform | Very swollen at top, top-shaped |
| Sweet potato (Convolvulaceae) | Tuberous adventitious root | Irregular swollen roots, no buds |
| Banyan (Moraceae) | Prop roots | Pillar-like roots hanging from branches |
| Maize (Poaceae) | Stilt roots | Roots from lower nodes entering soil obliquely |

**Stems**

| Specimen (family) | Modification | Identifying features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Potato (Solanaceae) | Stem tuber | "Eyes" (buds) in axils of scale leaves at nodes |
| Ginger (Zingiberaceae) | Rhizome | Horizontal, nodes and internodes, scale leaves, buds |
| *Colocasia* (Araceae) | Corm | Rounded, vertical, with nodes and buds |
| Onion (Amaryllidaceae) | Bulb | Reduced disc-like stem with fleshy scale leaves and adventitious roots |
| *Opuntia* (Cactaceae) | Phylloclade | Flat green stem; leaves reduced to spines |
| Grapevine (Vitaceae) | Stem tendril | Coiled tendril from a bud |
| *Citrus* (Rutaceae), *Bougainvillea* | Thorns | Hard pointed structures arising from axillary buds |

**Leaves**

| Specimen | Feature studied |
| --- | --- |
| Mango or peepal | Simple leaf, reticulate venation |
| Grass, banana | Parallel venation |
| Neem (Meliaceae) | Pinnately compound leaf |
| Pea (Fabaceae) | Leaflets modified into tendrils |
| *Opuntia* | Leaves modified into spines |
| *Nepenthes* (if available) | Leaf modified into a pitcher |
| Phyllotaxy: China rose (alternate), *Calotropis* (opposite), *Alstonia* (whorled) | Arrangement of leaves |

**Flower** (for example China rose, *Hibiscus rosa-sinensis*, Malvaceae, or mustard, Brassicaceae): note pedicel, thalamus, calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium; symmetry; aestivation; position of ovary; cut the ovary transversely to see placentation; write the floral formula.

**Inflorescence:** mustard (racemose), sunflower (capitulum, Asteraceae), coriander (umbel, Apiaceae), tulsi (verticillaster, Lamiaceae).

**Fruits:** tomato (berry), mango (drupe), orange (hesperidium), apple (pome), pea (legume), mustard (siliqua), cotton (capsule), wheat (caryopsis), custard apple (aggregate), jackfruit (multiple).

**Seeds:** gram or bean (dicot: two cotyledons, hilum, micropyle, no endosperm when mature); maize (monocot: one cotyledon/scutellum, large endosperm, coleoptile, coleorhiza). Soak seeds overnight before opening them.

## Observations

| No. | Specimen | Organ | Modification / type | Function | Family |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 |  |  |  |  |  |
| 2 |  |  |  |  |  |

## Result

The morphology of the given plant parts and their modifications was studied and recorded.

## Precautions

1. Look for nodes, buds and scale leaves before deciding whether a part is a stem or root.
2. Use fresh specimens where possible; soak seeds before opening.
3. Cut flowers and ovaries carefully with a sharp blade.
4. Draw neat, labelled diagrams.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is potato a stem and sweet potato a root?** Potato has nodes with buds (eyes); sweet potato has none.
2. **Name a fusiform root.** Radish.
3. **What is a phylloclade?** A flattened green stem that does photosynthesis, as in *Opuntia*.
4. **What type of placentation is seen in mustard?** Parietal.
5. **Why is apple a false fruit?** Its edible part develops from the thalamus, not the ovary.
6. **How does a maize grain differ from a gram seed?** Maize has one cotyledon and a large endosperm; gram has two cotyledons and no endosperm.

# Detailed study of frog using computer models

**Aim:** To study the external features and the internal organ systems of the frog using computer models, charts and preserved museum specimens, without dissection.

> Dissection of animals is no longer done for this practical; the frog is studied with software, models and charts as the syllabus directs. Follow your lab manual and your teacher.

## Principle

The frog is an **amphibian** (lives on land and in water) and a **vertebrate** (has a backbone). Its organ systems follow the same plan as in humans, so it is a simple model for learning body systems. The common Indian frog is the Indian bullfrog, *Hoplobatrachus tigerinus* (older books: *Rana tigrina*). Computer models let the student open each system on screen, rotate it and identify parts.

**Classification (outline):** Kingdom Animalia → Phylum Chordata → Class Amphibia → Order Anura (tailless amphibians).

## Requirements

Computer with frog anatomy software or a virtual dissection program, charts, models, preserved museum specimen.

## Procedure

1. Open the frog model and study the external features.
2. Open each system in turn: digestive, respiratory, circulatory, excretory, nervous, reproductive.
3. Identify the parts named below, rotate the model to see their positions, and note their functions.
4. Draw labelled diagrams of the external features, digestive system, heart and urinogenital system.

## Observations

**External features**

- Body divided into **head and trunk**; no neck and no tail in the adult.
- Skin smooth, moist and slippery due to mucus; can absorb water and exchange gases. Dorsal side olive-green with dark spots; ventral side pale yellow. Colour can change to match surroundings (camouflage).
- Head: mouth, a pair of **nostrils**, bulging **eyes** covered by a **nictitating membrane** in water, and a **tympanum** (eardrum) behind each eye.
- Forelimbs short with four digits; hindlimbs longer and stronger with five webbed digits for jumping and swimming.
- Male shows **vocal sacs** and a **copulatory pad** on the first digit of each forelimb; females have neither.

**Digestive system:** mouth → buccal cavity (bilobed tongue that can be flicked out to catch insects; teeth on upper jaw) → pharynx → short oesophagus → stomach → intestine → rectum → **cloaca** (common chamber for digestive, excretory and reproductive products). Liver with gall bladder; pancreas. Frog is carnivorous.

**Respiratory system:** breathes through the **skin** (cutaneous respiration, in water and during aestivation and hibernation), the **buccal cavity** and the **lungs** on land.

**Circulatory system:** closed system; **three-chambered heart** — two atria and one ventricle — with a **sinus venosus** joining the right atrium and a **conus arteriosus** leaving the ventricle. It has a **hepatic portal system** and a **renal portal system**. Lymphatic system present. RBCs are nucleated.

**Excretory system:** a pair of kidneys, ureters, cloaca and urinary bladder. The frog is **ureotelic** (excretes urea). In males the ureters also carry sperm (urinogenital ducts).

**Nervous system:** brain (forebrain with olfactory lobes and cerebral hemispheres; midbrain with optic lobes; hindbrain with cerebellum and medulla oblongata), spinal cord, **10 pairs of cranial nerves**. Sense organs: eyes, internal ears (hearing and balance), nasal epithelium, taste buds, touch receptors.

**Reproductive system:** sexes separate. Male: a pair of yellowish testes attached to the kidneys. Female: a pair of ovaries and oviducts opening into the cloaca. **Fertilisation is external** (in water); eggs hatch into **tadpoles**, which undergo **metamorphosis** into adult frogs.

**Other features:** cold-blooded (**poikilothermic**: body temperature follows the surroundings); escapes extreme heat by **aestivation** (summer sleep) and extreme cold by **hibernation** (winter sleep). Frogs eat insects and help control pests.

## Result

The external features and internal organ systems of the frog were studied using computer models and charts.

## Precautions

1. Identify each part from more than one view of the model.
2. Draw labelled diagrams in proportion.
3. Handle preserved specimens and their jars carefully.

## Viva questions

1. **How many chambers are in a frog's heart?** Three: two atria and one ventricle.
2. **What is the cloaca?** A common chamber into which digestive, excretory and reproductive tracts open.
3. **Name the modes of respiration in frog.** Cutaneous (skin), buccal and pulmonary (lungs).
4. **How can a male frog be recognised?** By vocal sacs and copulatory pads on the forelimbs.
5. **What are aestivation and hibernation?** Summer and winter sleep to escape extreme heat and cold.
6. **Why is the frog called poikilothermic?** Its body temperature changes with the surroundings.
practicals.title: Detailed study of frog using computer models

# Microscopic study and identification of tissues of stem, root, leaf, seed, fruit and flower

**Aim:** To identify the tissues in transverse sections (T.S.) of dicot and monocot stem, root and leaf, and in sections or preparations of seed, fruit and flower parts.

> Use prepared permanent slides or sections you cut and stained yourself. Follow your lab manual and your teacher.

## Principle

Each plant organ has a typical arrangement of tissues. Recognising this arrangement under the microscope identifies the organ and tells whether it is from a **dicot** or a **monocot**. Simple tissues are **parenchyma** (thin-walled, living), **collenchyma** (corners thickened, living) and **sclerenchyma** (thick lignified walls, dead); complex tissues are **xylem** (water conduction) and **phloem** (food conduction).

## Requirements

Permanent slides or freshly stained sections: T.S. of sunflower and maize stem, T.S. of bean (or sunflower) and maize root, T.S. of a dicot leaf (mango) and a monocot leaf (grass or maize), T.S. of an anther, T.S. of an ovary, a fruit wall section, a section of a seed (maize grain), microscope.

## Procedure

1. Focus each slide under low power and identify the overall plan.
2. Switch to high power to study particular tissues.
3. Compare with the identifying features below.
4. Draw an outline diagram (low power) and a cellular detail (high power), with labels.

## Identifying features

| Section | Identifying features |
| --- | --- |
| **Dicot stem (sunflower)** | Epidermis with hairs; collenchyma hypodermis; cortex; endodermis; pericycle (sclerenchyma patches); **vascular bundles in a ring**, conjoint, collateral, **open**, endarch; large pith |
| **Monocot stem (maize)** | Sclerenchyma hypodermis; ground tissue not divided; **many scattered bundles**, closed, each with a sclerenchyma **bundle sheath**; water cavity; no pith |
| **Dicot root (bean)** | Epiblema with root hairs; wide cortex; endodermis with **Casparian strips**; pericycle; **2–4 radial xylem bundles**, exarch; pith small or absent |
| **Monocot root (maize)** | Similar layers; **more than 6 xylem bundles** (polyarch), exarch; **large pith** |
| **Dicot leaf (dorsiventral)** | Upper epidermis with cuticle; **palisade** layer below it; **spongy** mesophyll with air spaces; more stomata in lower epidermis; vascular bundle in midrib with xylem towards upper side |
| **Monocot leaf (isobilateral)** | Mesophyll not divided; stomata on both surfaces; **bulliform cells** in upper epidermis; parallel bundles with bundle sheath |
| **Anther (flower)** | Four pollen sacs (tetrasporangiate) with wall layers (epidermis, endothecium, middle layers, tapetum) and pollen grains |
| **Ovary (flower)** | Ovary wall, locules, ovules attached to placenta (placentation visible) |
| **Fruit wall** | Pericarp of epicarp, mesocarp and endocarp; in drupes the endocarp is stony (sclereids) |
| **Seed (maize grain)** | Fused fruit wall and seed coat; aleurone layer; starchy endosperm; scutellum; embryo with coleoptile and coleorhiza |

## Observations

| Slide | Features observed | Identified as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A |  |  |
| B |  |  |
| C |  |  |

## Result

The given slides were identified as ______ on the basis of the features recorded above.

## Precautions

1. Start with low power to see the whole plan, then use high power.
2. Look at the arrangement of vascular bundles first; it is the quickest clue.
3. Draw proportionate, neatly labelled diagrams.
4. Handle permanent slides carefully and return them clean.

## Viva questions

1. **How do you identify a monocot stem?** Scattered, closed vascular bundles with bundle sheaths.
2. **What are Casparian strips?** Bands of suberin in the walls of root endodermis cells that control water entry.
3. **Why are root bundles called radial?** Xylem and phloem lie on different radii, alternating.
4. **What is exarch xylem?** Protoxylem lies towards the outside, as in roots.
5. **What are bulliform cells?** Large epidermal cells in grass leaves that let the leaf roll up when water is short.
6. **Name the nutritive layer of the anther wall.** Tapetum.
practicals.title: Microscopic study and identification of tissues of stem, root, leaf, seed, fruit and flower

# Identification of bones

**Aim:** To identify the bones of the human skeleton and study their main features.

> Use articulated and disarticulated human skeletons or models available in the laboratory. Follow your lab manual and your teacher.

## Principle

The adult human skeleton has **206 bones**. It is divided into the **axial skeleton** (80 bones along the central axis: skull, vertebral column, sternum, ribs) and the **appendicular skeleton** (126 bones: limbs and girdles). A bone is identified by its shape, size and special features (processes, holes, joint surfaces). Bones support the body, protect organs, allow movement with muscles, store calcium and phosphate, and their red marrow forms blood cells.

**Types by shape:** long (femur, humerus), short (carpals), flat (skull bones, sternum, ribs), irregular (vertebrae), sesamoid (patella).

## Requirements

Human skeleton or models, individual bones, charts.

## Procedure

1. Study the articulated skeleton to see where each bone lies.
2. Pick up each bone, note its shape and identifying features, and decide its name (and side for paired bones).
3. Draw it and label the features.

## Bones and identifying features

**Axial skeleton (80)**

| Bone | Number | Identifying features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Skull** | 22 (8 cranial + 14 facial) | Cranium encloses the brain; lower jaw (**mandible**) is the only movable skull bone; **foramen magnum** at the base for the spinal cord; joins the vertebral column through two **occipital condyles** (dicondylic) |
| Ear ossicles | 6 (3 per ear) | Malleus, incus, stapes (stapes is the smallest bone) |
| Hyoid | 1 | U-shaped bone in the neck, at the base of the buccal cavity |
| **Vertebral column** | 26 | Cervical 7, thoracic 12, lumbar 5, sacrum 1 (5 fused), coccyx 1 (4 fused) |

# Determination of blood group

**Aim:** To determine the ABO and Rh blood group of a given blood sample by the slide agglutination method.

> Handle blood as possibly infectious. Use a sterile, disposable lancet for each person, wear gloves, and discard sharps and blood-stained material as your laboratory directs. Follow your lab manual and your teacher.

## Principle

The ABO group depends on the **antigens** present on the surface of red blood cells (RBCs). When RBCs carrying an antigen meet the matching **antibody** (antiserum), they clump together. This clumping is called **agglutination** and is visible to the naked eye.

| Antiserum | Contains | Clumps RBCs carrying |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Anti-A | Antibody against antigen A | A antigen (groups A and AB) |
| Anti-B | Antibody against antigen B | B antigen (groups B and AB) |
| Anti-D | Antibody against Rh (D) antigen | Rh-positive RBCs |

## Requirements

Anti-A, anti-B and anti-D antisera, clean glass slide (or a white tile), sterile lancet, 70% alcohol (spirit) swab, cotton, separate mixing sticks or toothpicks, marker pen, gloves.

## Procedure

1. Mark three areas on the slide as A, B and D.
2. Clean the tip of the ring finger with a spirit swab and let it dry.
3. Prick the fingertip with a sterile lancet; wipe away the first drop.
4. Place one drop of blood in each of the three areas.
5. Add one drop of anti-A to area A, anti-B to area B and anti-D to area D.
6. Mix each with a separate clean stick, spreading slightly.
7. Rock the slide gently and look for agglutination within about 1–2 minutes (anti-D may take a little longer); view against a white background.
8. Press cotton on the pricked finger until bleeding stops.

```text
   [ A ]          [ B ]          [ D ]
 blood+anti-A   blood+anti-B   blood+anti-D
  clumps?         clumps?        clumps?
```

## Observations

| Anti-A | Anti-B | Blood group |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Agglutination | No agglutination | A |
| No agglutination | Agglutination | B |
| Agglutination | Agglutination | AB |
| No agglutination | No agglutination | O |

| Anti-D | Rh type |
| --- | --- |
| Agglutination | Rh-positive |
| No agglutination | Rh-negative |

**Recorded:** Anti-A ______, anti-B ______, anti-D ______.

## Result

The blood group of the given sample is ______ (Rh ______).

## Precautions

1. Use a fresh sterile lancet for every person; never share.
2. Use separate sticks for each antiserum to avoid mixing.
3. Do not take too large a drop of blood; it may hide the clumps.
4. Read the result in time; drying at the edges can look like clumping.
5. Keep antisera refrigerated and check that they are within date.
6. Dispose of sharps and blood-stained material safely.

## Viva questions

1. **What is agglutination?** Clumping of RBCs when their antigen meets the matching antibody.
2. **Which group is the universal donor?** O (Rh-negative is preferred in emergencies).
3. **Which group is the universal recipient?** AB.
4. **Who discovered the ABO system?** Karl Landsteiner.
5. **What is the danger of Rh incompatibility in pregnancy?** An Rh-negative mother's antibodies can destroy the RBCs of an Rh-positive fetus in a later pregnancy (erythroblastosis fetalis).
6. **Which antibodies are present in the plasma of group O?** Both anti-A and anti-B.

# Determination of blood pressure

**Aim:** To measure the arterial blood pressure of a person using a sphygmomanometer by the auscultatory method.

> Follow your lab manual and your teacher. Many laboratories now use aneroid or digital instruments; the principle is the same.

## Principle

**Blood pressure (BP)** is the pressure exerted by blood on the walls of the arteries. It is highest during ventricular contraction (**systolic pressure**) and lowest during relaxation (**diastolic pressure**), written as systolic/diastolic in **mmHg**, for example 120/80 mmHg.

A **sphygmomanometer** has an inflatable cuff, a rubber bulb with a valve, and a manometer (mercury column, aneroid dial or digital sensor). The cuff squeezes the **brachial artery** of the upper arm. When the cuff pressure is above systolic, the artery is closed and no sound is heard. As the pressure is released, blood begins to spurt through the partly opened artery, producing tapping sounds heard with a stethoscope, the **Korotkoff sounds**:

- The pressure at the **first clear tapping sound** = **systolic pressure**.
- The pressure at which the sounds **disappear** = **diastolic pressure**.

```text
 cuff pressure
   ^
 140|  silence (artery closed)
 120|  ---- first tapping sound  = SYSTOLIC
    |  sounds continue as pressure falls
  80|  ---- sounds disappear     = DIASTOLIC
    |  silence (blood flows freely)
    +-------------------------------> time (pressure released slowly)
```

**Derived values**

- **Pulse pressure** = systolic − diastolic (normally about 40 mmHg).
- **Mean arterial pressure (MAP)** ≈ diastolic + ⅓ × pulse pressure.

## Requirements

Sphygmomanometer with a cuff of correct size, stethoscope, chair and table.

## Procedure

1. Let the subject sit quietly for about 5 minutes, back supported, feet on the floor, arm resting on a table at the level of the heart. No smoking, coffee or exercise just before the test.
2. Wrap the deflated cuff snugly round the bare upper arm, its lower edge about 2–3 cm above the elbow crease, with the centre of the bladder over the brachial artery.
3. **Palpatory estimate:** feel the radial pulse at the wrist, inflate the cuff until the pulse disappears, and note this pressure; deflate fully. This avoids missing the first sound.
4. Place the stethoscope diaphragm over the brachial artery at the inner side of the elbow (below the cuff, not under it).
5. Inflate the cuff to about 20–30 mmHg above the palpatory value.
6. Open the valve and release pressure slowly, about 2–3 mmHg per second.
7. Note the pressure at the first clear tapping sound (systolic) and when the sounds disappear (diastolic).
8. Deflate completely. Wait 1–2 minutes and repeat; take the average of two readings.

## Observations and calculations

| Reading | Systolic (mmHg) | Diastolic (mmHg) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 |  |  |
| 2 |  |  |
| Mean |  |  |

**Worked example.** Systolic 120 mmHg, diastolic 80 mmHg → pulse pressure = 120 − 80 = **40 mmHg**; MAP ≈ 80 + 40/3 ≈ **93 mmHg**.

**Reference values for adults:** normal about 120/80 mmHg; persistently 140/90 mmHg or above suggests hypertension (diagnosis is made by a doctor on repeated readings).

## Result

The blood pressure of the subject was ______ / ______ mmHg; pulse pressure ______ mmHg; mean arterial pressure ______ mmHg.

## Precautions

1. The subject must be relaxed and seated; posture and activity change BP.
2. Keep the arm at heart level.
3. Use the correct cuff size; a small cuff gives falsely high readings.
4. Release pressure slowly and steadily.
5. Do not keep the cuff inflated for long; it is uncomfortable and changes readings.
6. Keep a mercury instrument upright and read at eye level.

## Viva questions

1. **Define systolic and diastolic pressure.** Pressure in arteries during ventricular contraction and relaxation respectively.
2. **What are Korotkoff sounds?** Tapping sounds of blood spurting through a partly compressed artery.
3. **Which artery is used?** The brachial artery.
4. **What is the normal pulse pressure?** About 40 mmHg.
5. **Why is the palpatory method done first?** To avoid missing the true systolic pressure because of a silent gap.
6. **Name two factors that raise BP.** Exercise, stress or anxiety (also smoking, salt intake).

# Determination of tidal volume

**Aim:** To determine the tidal volume (and, where possible, vital capacity) of a person using a spirometer, and to calculate the minute volume.

> Use a fresh disposable mouthpiece for each person. Stop if the subject feels dizzy. Follow your lab manual and your teacher.

## Principle

**Tidal volume (TV)** is the volume of air breathed in or out in one normal, quiet breath, about **500 ml** in a healthy adult. It is measured with a **spirometer**, a device that records the volume of air breathed.

Common laboratory types:

- **Wet (water-sealed) spirometer:** an inverted bell floats in water; air breathed into it lifts the bell, and the rise on a calibrated scale gives the volume.
- **Hand-held or dry spirometer:** air blown through it turns a dial or a turbine that shows the volume; electronic spirometers display the value directly.

Related values:

- **Vital capacity (VC)** = maximum air breathed out after a maximum breath in = TV + IRV + ERV.
- **Minute volume** = tidal volume × breaths per minute (normal rate 12–16 per minute).

## Requirements

Spirometer (wet, dry or electronic), disposable mouthpieces, nose clip, stopwatch.

## Procedure

**Tidal volume**

1. Set the spirometer to zero and fit a fresh mouthpiece.
2. Let the subject sit or stand upright and breathe normally for a minute.
3. Put on the nose clip so that air does not pass through the nose.
4. After a normal breath in, the subject places the mouthpiece in the mouth and breathes out **normally** (not forcibly) into the spirometer.
5. Read the volume. Repeat three times and take the average.
6. Count the subject's breaths per minute at rest with a stopwatch, without telling the subject (people change their breathing when watched).

**Vital capacity (if asked)**

1. The subject takes the deepest possible breath in.
2. Then breathes out as much air as possible, as fast as possible, into the spirometer.
3. Read and repeat three times; take the highest value.

## Observations and calculations

| Trial | Tidal volume (ml) | Vital capacity (ml) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 |  |  |
| 2 |  |  |
| 3 |  |  |
| Mean / best |  |  |

Respiratory rate = ______ breaths per minute.

**Minute volume = TV × respiratory rate.**

**Worked example.** TV readings 480, 500 and 520 ml → mean **500 ml**. Respiratory rate 14 per minute → minute volume = 500 × 14 = **7,000 ml/min (7 L/min)**.

## Result

The tidal volume of the subject was ______ ml, the vital capacity ______ ml and the minute volume ______ L/min.

## Precautions

1. Use a fresh mouthpiece for each subject.
2. Use a nose clip so that no air escapes through the nose.
3. For tidal volume, breathing must be normal and quiet, not forced.
4. Make sure the lips seal around the mouthpiece.
5. Take several readings and average them.
6. Allow rest between attempts at vital capacity to avoid dizziness.

## Viva questions

1. **Define tidal volume.** The volume of air breathed in or out in one normal breath, about 500 ml.
2. **What is vital capacity?** Maximum air breathed out after a maximum breath in (TV + IRV + ERV).
3. **What is residual volume and can a spirometer measure it?** Air left in the lungs after forced expiration, about 1,100–1,200 ml; a simple spirometer cannot measure it.
4. **Why is a nose clip used?** To prevent air passing through the nose.
5. **What is minute volume?** Tidal volume × breaths per minute, about 6–8 L/min.
6. **Name a factor that lowers vital capacity.** Lung disease such as asthma or emphysema (also poor posture or smoking).

6. Plantae: eukaryotic, multicellular, chlorophyll, cellulose wall, autotrophic; algae, mosses, ferns, gymnosperms, angiosperms; alternation of generations. Few partial heterotrophs (Cuscuta, insectivorous plants).
