# Unit 3: Excretion, neural control, chemical coordination and human reproduction

This is the largest unit. It covers how the body removes wastes (kidneys), how it sends fast messages (nerves) and slower chemical messages (hormones), and how humans reproduce. Kidney function decides how fast many drugs leave the body; nerves and hormones are the targets of a large part of pharmacology; and hormones of reproduction are the basis of contraceptive pills.

## 3.1 Excretory products and their elimination

**Excretion** is the removal of waste products of metabolism (body chemistry) from the body. The main wastes are **nitrogenous wastes** formed when proteins and nucleic acids are broken down, plus CO2, excess water and salts.

### Modes of excretion

Animals are grouped by the main nitrogenous waste they make:

| Mode | Main waste | Toxicity and water need | Found in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Ammonotelism** | Ammonia | Most toxic; needs a lot of water to wash it out; very soluble, so it diffuses out easily | Bony fish, aquatic amphibians, aquatic insects |
| **Ureotelism** | Urea | Less toxic; moderate water needed; made in the liver from ammonia | Mammals (including humans), many terrestrial amphibians, marine fish |
| **Uricotelism** | Uric acid | Least toxic; removed as a paste or pellet with very little water; saves water | Reptiles, birds, land snails, insects |

**Excretory organs in different animals:** flame cells (protonephridia) in flatworms like *Planaria*; nephridia in earthworm; Malpighian tubules in insects such as cockroach; antennal (green) glands in prawn; kidneys in vertebrates.

**Other organs that help excretion in humans:** lungs (CO2, water vapour), liver (bile pigments bilirubin and biliverdin, cholesterol, some drugs and vitamins), skin (sweat with water, salt, a little urea; sebum).

### Human excretory system — structure

```text
        kidney (left)          kidney (right, slightly lower)
              \                    /
              ureter            ureter
                \                /
                 urinary bladder (stores urine)
                        |
                     urethra  --> outside
```

- **Kidneys:** a pair of bean-shaped, reddish-brown organs on either side of the backbone, between the last thoracic and third lumbar vertebrae, each about 10–12 cm long and 120–170 g. On the inner concave side is a notch, the **hilum**, where the ureter, blood vessels and nerves enter or leave. Inside the hilum is a funnel-shaped space, the **renal pelvis**.
- A section of the kidney shows an outer **cortex** and inner **medulla**; the medulla is divided into cone-shaped **medullary pyramids** that open into the **calyces**. Extensions of the cortex between the pyramids are the **renal columns (columns of Bertini)**.
- Each kidney has about **one million nephrons**, the structural and functional units.

### Structure of a nephron

```text
 afferent arteriole -> GLOMERULUS (tuft of capillaries) -> efferent arteriole
                          inside
                   BOWMAN'S CAPSULE  } together = Malpighian body
                          |            (renal corpuscle)
                 Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT)  - in cortex
                          |
                 Loop of Henle (descending + ascending limbs) - dips into medulla
                          |
                 Distal convoluted tubule (DCT)    - in cortex
                          |
                 Collecting duct (shared by many nephrons)
                          |
                 renal pelvis -> ureter
```

- The efferent arteriole forms a capillary network around the tubule (**peritubular capillaries**); around the loop of Henle it forms the **vasa recta**.
- **Cortical nephrons** (most) have short loops that barely enter the medulla. **Juxtamedullary nephrons** have very long loops reaching deep into the medulla; they help make concentrated urine.

### Urine formation

Urine is formed in three steps:

**1. Glomerular filtration (ultrafiltration).** Blood pressure in the glomerulus forces water and small dissolved substances (glucose, amino acids, salts, urea) out of the blood into Bowman's capsule. Blood cells and plasma proteins stay behind. The filter has three layers: capillary endothelium, basement membrane and the **podocytes** (cells of the capsule) with tiny slits between their foot processes.

- **Glomerular filtration rate (GFR)** — volume filtered by both kidneys per minute ≈ **125 ml/min**, about **180 litres per day**.

**2. Reabsorption.** About **99%** of the filtrate is taken back into blood as it flows along the tubule. Glucose, amino acids and Na+ are reabsorbed actively (using energy); water passively.

| Part | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| PCT | Most reabsorption: almost all glucose and amino acids, about 70–80% of salts and water; H+ and NH3 secreted to keep blood pH balanced |
| Descending limb of Henle's loop | Permeable to water, almost not to salts — filtrate becomes concentrated |
| Ascending limb | Impermeable to water; salts move out — filtrate becomes dilute |
| DCT | Some Na+ and water reabsorbed under hormone control; H+ and K+ secreted |
| Collecting duct | Large amounts of water reabsorbed under the control of **ADH**, giving concentrated urine |

**3. Tubular secretion.** Cells of the tubule add substances from blood to the filtrate: H+, K+, ammonia, creatinine and many drugs (penicillin, for example). This helps keep ion and acid–base balance.

The **counter-current mechanism** of the loop of Henle and vasa recta (fluid flowing in opposite directions in neighbouring limbs) builds up a high salt concentration in the deep medulla, so that water can be drawn out of the collecting duct and urine can be up to about four times more concentrated than the filtrate.

**Normal urine:** about 1–1.5 litres a day, light yellow, slightly acidic (pH about 6), with about 25–30 g urea a day. Glucose in urine (**glycosuria**) and ketone bodies (**ketonuria**) suggest diabetes mellitus.

### Renin–angiotensin system

(The syllabus prints "Rennin". **Renin**, with one n, is the kidney enzyme; **rennin** is the milk-curdling enzyme of the stomach. Do not mix them up in the exam.)

```text
 Fall in blood pressure / blood flow / GFR
        |
        v
 Juxtaglomerular (JG) cells of the kidney release RENIN
        |
 ANGIOTENSINOGEN (plasma protein from liver) ---renin---> ANGIOTENSIN I
        |
        |  angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), mainly in lungs
        v
 ANGIOTENSIN II (active)
    |                                   |
    v                                   v
 constricts blood vessels         adrenal cortex releases ALDOSTERONE
 (raises BP)                         -> Na+ and water reabsorbed in DCT
                                     -> blood volume and BP rise
        |
        v
 GFR and blood pressure return to normal (negative feedback)
```

- The **juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA)** is a special region where the DCT touches the afferent arteriole; it senses falling GFR.
- **ADH (antidiuretic hormone, vasopressin)** from the posterior pituitary is released when the body loses water; it makes the DCT and collecting duct reabsorb more water, so less urine forms.
- **Atrial natriuretic factor (ANF)**, released by the heart when blood pressure rises, dilates vessels and opposes the renin–angiotensin system.
- Pharmacy link: **ACE inhibitors** (such as enalapril) lower blood pressure by blocking the conversion of angiotensin I to II.

**Disorders:** **uraemia** (urea builds up in blood; treated by **haemodialysis**, an artificial kidney), **renal calculi** (kidney stones, often calcium oxalate), **glomerulonephritis** (inflammation of glomeruli).

## 3.2 Neural control and coordination

**Coordination** is how organs work together. The **nervous system** gives fast, point-to-point control through electrical impulses.

### Definition and classification of the nervous system

The **nervous system** is the network of neurons (nerve cells) that receives information, processes it and sends instructions to muscles and glands.

```text
                  HUMAN NERVOUS SYSTEM
           ______________|________________
          |                               |
  CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM          PERIPHERAL NERVOUS SYSTEM
  (CNS): brain + spinal cord      (PNS): nerves outside the CNS
  (processing and control)        12 pairs cranial + 31 pairs spinal nerves
                                    _______________|_______________
                                   |                               |
                          AFFERENT (sensory) fibres      EFFERENT (motor) fibres
                          carry impulses TO the CNS      carry impulses FROM the CNS
                                                      __________|__________
                                                     |                     |
                                              SOMATIC system       AUTONOMIC system
                                              (to skeletal         (to smooth muscle,
                                               muscles; voluntary)  heart, glands; involuntary)
                                                               ______|______
                                                              |             |
                                                       SYMPATHETIC   PARASYMPATHETIC
                                                      ("fight or     ("rest and
                                                        flight")       digest")
```

The **visceral nervous system** is the part of the PNS that connects the CNS with internal organs (viscera).

### Structure of a neuron

A **neuron** is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system.

```text
 dendrites   cell body (cyton)         axon                axon terminals
   \|/    [ nucleus + Nissl's  ]========[myelin]=[myelin]=====< synaptic knobs
   -O-    [ granules in        ]          node of Ranvier       (neurotransmitter
   /|\    [ cytoplasm          ]          (gap in myelin)        vesicles)
```

| Part | Feature and role |
| --- | --- |
| **Cell body (cyton)** | Has the nucleus, cytoplasm, organelles and **Nissl's granules** (groups of ribosomes) |
| **Dendrites** | Short branched processes; carry impulses **towards** the cell body |
| **Axon** | Single long process; carries impulses **away** from the cell body; ends in branches with **synaptic knobs** that hold **neurotransmitters** (chemical messengers) |
| **Myelin sheath** | Fatty covering formed by **Schwann cells** in the PNS; insulates the axon |
| **Nodes of Ranvier** | Gaps in the myelin sheath |

**Types by number of processes:** **multipolar** (one axon, two or more dendrites; most common, in the brain), **bipolar** (one axon, one dendrite; retina of the eye), **unipolar** (cell body with one process; embryonic stage). **Myelinated** fibres (spinal and cranial nerves) conduct faster than **non-myelinated** fibres (autonomic and somatic nervous system in parts).

### Generation and conduction of a nerve impulse

**Resting state.** The axon membrane at rest is **polarised**: the outside is positively charged and the inside negatively charged. The **resting membrane potential** is about **−70 mV**. It is kept by:

- The **sodium–potassium pump**, which uses ATP to push **3 Na+ out for every 2 K+ in**.
- The membrane being more permeable to K+ than to Na+, so the inside stays rich in K+ and negatively charged proteins, and the outside rich in Na+.

**Action potential (nerve impulse)**

```text
 1. Stimulus at a point -> Na+ channels open -> Na+ rushes IN
    -> inside becomes positive, outside negative = DEPOLARISATION
       (this reversed state is the action potential)
 2. Na+ channels close, K+ channels open -> K+ moves OUT
    -> resting polarity restored = REPOLARISATION
 3. Na+/K+ pump restores the original ion distribution
 4. The depolarised spot triggers the next spot -> the impulse travels
    along the axon in one direction
```

In **myelinated** fibres the impulse jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next (**saltatory conduction**), which is much faster.

**Synapse.** A **synapse** is the junction where an impulse passes from one neuron to the next.

- **Electrical synapse:** membranes very close; current flows directly; very fast but rare.
- **Chemical synapse:** a gap, the **synaptic cleft**. The impulse reaching the axon terminal releases a **neurotransmitter** (such as **acetylcholine**) from vesicles. It crosses the cleft and binds to **receptors** on the next membrane, opening ion channels and starting a new impulse. Many drugs act at synapses by copying, blocking or prolonging neurotransmitters.

### Structure of the brain and spinal cord

**Protective coverings:** the CNS is protected by the skull and the backbone, and by three membranes, the **meninges** — outer **dura mater**, middle **arachnoid mater**, inner **pia mater**. The space between the arachnoid and pia contains **cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)**, which cushions the brain.

**Main parts of the brain**

```text
 FOREBRAIN  : cerebrum, thalamus, hypothalamus
 MIDBRAIN   : between thalamus/hypothalamus and pons (corpora quadrigemina)
 HINDBRAIN  : pons, cerebellum, medulla oblongata
 BRAINSTEM  = midbrain + pons + medulla oblongata (connects brain to spinal cord)
```

- **Cerebrum** — largest part; split into left and right **cerebral hemispheres** by a deep groove, joined by a thick band of nerve fibres, the **corpus callosum**. Its outer layer, the **cerebral cortex**, is **grey matter** (cell bodies) thrown into folds; the inner part is **white matter** (myelinated fibres).
- **Thalamus** — major relay centre for sensory and motor signals, wrapped by the cerebrum.
- **Hypothalamus** — at the base of the thalamus.
- **Cerebellum** — "little brain", at the back below the cerebrum, with a very folded surface.
- **Medulla oblongata** — lowest part, continuous with the spinal cord.

### Functions of the main brain regions

| Region | Functions |
| --- | --- |
| **Cerebrum** | Seat of intelligence, memory, thinking, reasoning, learning and voluntary actions; sensory areas receive sensations (touch, pain, temperature, sight, hearing); motor areas control voluntary muscles; **association areas** handle intersensory links, memory and communication (speech) |
| **Cerebellum** | Coordinates voluntary movements; keeps **balance (equilibrium)** and **posture**; makes movements smooth and precise |
| **Hypothalamus** | Controls body **temperature**, **hunger**, **thirst** and urge to eat and drink; links nerves and hormones by releasing **hypothalamic hormones** that control the pituitary; with the limbic system it is involved in emotions, sexual behaviour and motivation |
| **Medulla oblongata** | Centres for **breathing**, **heart rate and blood pressure** (cardiovascular reflexes), gastric secretion; reflexes of swallowing, coughing, sneezing and vomiting |

Damage to the medulla can be fatal because breathing and heartbeat are controlled there.

### Spinal cord

- A long cylindrical cord inside the **vertebral canal** of the backbone, from the medulla oblongata to about the level of the first or second lumbar vertebra; it gives off **31 pairs of spinal nerves**.
- In cross-section: an inner **H-shaped (butterfly-shaped) grey matter** and outer **white matter**. A small **central canal** filled with CSF runs through the middle.
- Sensory (afferent) fibres enter through the **dorsal root** (which carries a swelling, the dorsal root ganglion); motor (efferent) fibres leave through the **ventral root**.
- Functions: carries impulses up to the brain and down from it; centre for **reflex actions**.

**Reflex action and reflex arc.** A **reflex** is an automatic, quick, involuntary response to a stimulus, controlled by the spinal cord without needing the brain (for example the knee-jerk reflex or pulling the hand back from a hot object).

```text
 stimulus -> receptor -> afferent (sensory) neuron -> spinal cord
   (interneuron in some reflexes) -> efferent (motor) neuron -> effector
   (muscle or gland) -> response
```

## 3.3 Chemical coordination and regulation

**Hormones** are chemicals produced in very small amounts by **endocrine glands** (ductless glands), released directly into the blood and acting on distant **target organs**. Endocrine control is slower than nerve control but lasts longer. Glands with ducts (salivary, sweat) are **exocrine**.

```text
 HYPOTHALAMUS (releasing and inhibiting hormones)
        |
 PITUITARY ("master gland")
   |      |       |        |
 thyroid adrenal ovary/   other targets
         cortex  testis
```

### Endocrine glands, their secretions and functions

| Gland (location) | Hormone | Main function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Hypothalamus** (base of brain) | Releasing hormones (e.g. GnRH — gonadotrophin-releasing hormone) and inhibiting hormones (e.g. somatostatin) | Start or stop secretion of pituitary hormones |
| **Pituitary — anterior lobe (adenohypophysis)** (in a bony cavity below the brain) | Growth hormone (GH) | Body growth; too much in childhood → **gigantism**, in adults → **acromegaly**; too little → **pituitary dwarfism** |
| | Prolactin (PRL) | Growth of mammary glands and milk formation |
| | Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) | Stimulates the thyroid |
| | Adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH) | Stimulates the adrenal cortex to make glucocorticoids |
| | Luteinising hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) (gonadotrophins) | Control testes and ovaries; LH causes ovulation |
| Pituitary — intermediate lobe | Melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH) | Skin pigment cells |
| **Pituitary — posterior lobe (neurohypophysis)** (stores hormones made by the hypothalamus) | **Oxytocin** | Contraction of the uterus at childbirth; milk ejection |
| | **ADH (vasopressin)** | Water reabsorption in kidney; deficiency → **diabetes insipidus** (large volumes of dilute urine) |
| **Pineal gland** (top of forebrain) | Melatonin | Sleep–wake (24-hour) rhythm |
| **Thyroid** (neck, two lobes either side of the trachea) | Thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) — need **iodine** | Basal metabolic rate, growth, development; too little in a child → **cretinism**, in adults → **myxoedema**; iodine lack → **goitre** (enlarged thyroid); too much → **Graves' disease** (exophthalmic goitre) |
| | Thyrocalcitonin | Lowers blood calcium |
| **Parathyroid** (four, behind the thyroid) | Parathyroid hormone (PTH) | Raises blood calcium (from bone, kidney, gut) |
| **Thymus** (chest, behind sternum) | Thymosins | Development of T lymphocytes (immunity); shrinks in old age |
| **Adrenal gland — cortex** (on top of each kidney) | Glucocorticoids (mainly **cortisol**) | Raise blood glucose, reduce inflammation and immune response |
| | Mineralocorticoids (mainly **aldosterone**) | Na+ and water retention, K+ loss |
| | Small amounts of androgens | Some sex characters |
| **Adrenal gland — medulla** | **Adrenaline (epinephrine)** and noradrenaline — "emergency hormones" | "Fight or flight": faster heart, raised BP, more blood glucose, dilated pupils and airways |
| **Pancreas — islets of Langerhans** (α and β cells) | **Insulin** (β cells) | Lowers blood glucose (cells take up glucose; liver stores it as glycogen); lack → **diabetes mellitus** |
| | **Glucagon** (α cells) | Raises blood glucose (breaks down liver glycogen) |
| **Testes** | Testosterone (androgens, from Leydig cells) | Male sex organs, sperm production, male secondary sexual characters |
| **Ovaries** | Oestrogens (from growing follicles) | Female sex organs, secondary characters, growth of endometrium |
| | Progesterone (from corpus luteum) | Prepares and maintains the uterus for pregnancy |
| Others: heart, kidney, gut | ANF (heart); erythropoietin (kidney, stimulates RBC formation); gastrin, secretin, cholecystokinin (gut, control digestive secretions) | |

Adrenal cortex deficiency causes **Addison's disease**; excess cortisol causes **Cushing's syndrome**.

**How hormones act:** they bind to specific **receptors** — protein-type hormones on the cell membrane (using second messengers such as cyclic AMP), and steroid and thyroid hormones on receptors inside the cell that change gene activity.

## 3.4 Human reproduction

Humans reproduce **sexually** and are **viviparous** (give birth to young). Reproduction involves forming gametes (sperm and ova), fertilisation, development of the embryo, and birth.

### Male reproductive system (in the pelvic region)

```text
 TESTES (in scrotum) -> seminiferous tubules -> rete testis
   -> vasa efferentia -> EPIDIDYMIS -> VAS DEFERENS
   -> joins the duct of the SEMINAL VESICLE -> EJACULATORY DUCT
   -> URETHRA (through the prostate) -> PENIS -> outside
```

| Part | Feature and role |
| --- | --- |
| **Testes** (pair) | Primary sex organs; in the **scrotum**, outside the abdomen, which keeps them about **2–2.5 °C below body temperature**, needed for sperm formation; each has about 250 lobules with 1–3 **seminiferous tubules** each |
| **Seminiferous tubules** | Lined by **spermatogonia** (cells that form sperm) and **Sertoli cells** (nourish the developing sperm) |
| **Leydig (interstitial) cells** | Between the tubules; secrete **testosterone** |
| **Accessory ducts** | Rete testis, vasa efferentia, **epididymis** (stores and matures sperm), **vas deferens**, ejaculatory duct |
| **Urethra** | Common passage for urine and semen, opens at the tip of the penis |
| **Penis** | External copulatory organ |
| **Accessory glands** | **Seminal vesicles** (pair), **prostate gland**, **bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands** (pair); their secretions form **seminal plasma**, rich in fructose, calcium and enzymes |

**Semen** = sperm + seminal plasma.

### Female reproductive system (in the pelvic region)

```text
            fimbriae      fimbriae
   ovary  (infundibulum) (infundibulum)  ovary
     \     ampulla          ampulla      /
      \    isthmus          isthmus     /
       \________ UTERUS (womb) ________/
                    |
                 CERVIX (cervical canal)
                    |
                 VAGINA -> external opening
```

| Part | Feature and role |
| --- | --- |
| **Ovaries** (pair) | Primary female sex organs; produce **ova** and the hormones oestrogen and progesterone; each about 2–4 cm |
| **Oviducts (fallopian tubes)** | About 10–12 cm; parts: funnel-shaped **infundibulum** with finger-like **fimbriae** that collect the ovum at ovulation, wider **ampulla** (usual site of fertilisation) and narrow **isthmus** joining the uterus |
| **Uterus (womb)** | Pear-shaped, hollow; wall of three layers: outer **perimetrium**, thick muscular **myometrium** (strong contractions in childbirth) and inner glandular **endometrium** (changes during the menstrual cycle; the embryo implants here) |
| **Cervix** | Lower narrow part of the uterus, opening into the vagina; together they form the **birth canal** |
| **Vagina** | Muscular tube to the outside |
| **External genitalia (vulva)** | Mons pubis, labia majora, labia minora, hymen, clitoris |
| **Mammary glands** (pair) | Accessory glands with glandular tissue in lobes; produce milk after childbirth |

### Gametogenesis

**Gametogenesis** is the formation of gametes. It needs **meiosis**, a special cell division that halves the chromosome number: a human body cell is **diploid (2n = 46 chromosomes)**; gametes are **haploid (n = 23)**.

### Spermatogenesis (in the seminiferous tubules, starts at puberty)

```text
 Spermatogonium (2n)         -- mitosis, many cells
        |
 Primary spermatocyte (2n)
        |  MEIOSIS I
        v
 2 Secondary spermatocytes (n)
        |  MEIOSIS II
        v
 4 Spermatids (n)
        |  SPERMIOGENESIS (change of shape, no division)
        v
 4 Spermatozoa (sperm, n)  -> released into the tubule (spermiation)
```

**Hormonal control:** at puberty the hypothalamus increases **GnRH**, which makes the anterior pituitary release **LH** and **FSH**. LH acts on Leydig cells to make testosterone; FSH acts on Sertoli cells to support spermiogenesis.

**Structure of a sperm:** head (with the haploid nucleus and the **acrosome**, a cap of enzymes that helps penetrate the ovum), neck, **middle piece** (many mitochondria, energy for movement) and **tail** (movement). A man releases about 200–300 million sperm in one ejaculation.

### Oogenesis (in the ovary, starts before birth)

```text
 Oogonia (2n)  -- formed in the fetal ovary; no new oogonia after birth
        |
 Primary oocyte (2n) -- starts meiosis I, then ARRESTS in prophase I
        |               (inside a primary follicle) until puberty
        |  at puberty, each cycle: meiosis I completes in one follicle
        v
 Secondary oocyte (n) + first polar body (small, n)
        |  ovulation (secondary oocyte released, arrested in meiosis II)
        |  MEIOSIS II completes only if a sperm enters
        v
 Ovum (n) + second polar body (n)
```

**Follicle development:** primary follicle → secondary follicle (more granulosa cell layers and a theca) → tertiary follicle (fluid-filled cavity, the **antrum**) → mature **Graafian follicle**, which ruptures at ovulation. The ruptured follicle becomes the **corpus luteum**.

| Spermatogenesis | Oogenesis |
| --- | --- |
| In testes | In ovaries |
| Starts at puberty, continues through life | Starts before birth; one oocyte matures each cycle from puberty to menopause |
| One primary spermatocyte → **4 sperm** | One primary oocyte → **1 ovum** + polar bodies |
| Divisions equal | Cytoplasm divides unequally (polar bodies are tiny) |
| Gametes motile | Ovum non-motile, large, with stored food |

### Menstrual cycle

The **menstrual cycle** is the cycle of changes in the ovary and uterus of female primates, about **28–29 days** long. The first cycle is called **menarche** (at puberty); cycles stop at about 50 years (**menopause**).

```text
 Day  1-5   MENSTRUAL PHASE: endometrium breaks down; bleeding
             (menstrual flow) for 3-5 days
 Day  6-13  FOLLICULAR (PROLIFERATIVE) PHASE: FSH and LH rise; follicle
             grows into a Graafian follicle; it secretes OESTROGEN;
             endometrium regenerates and thickens
 Day 14     OVULATION: LH reaches a peak (LH surge) -> Graafian follicle
             ruptures -> secondary oocyte released
 Day 15-28  LUTEAL (SECRETORY) PHASE: ruptured follicle becomes the
             CORPUS LUTEUM, which secretes much PROGESTERONE; endometrium
             becomes thick and glandular, ready for implantation
 If no fertilisation: corpus luteum degenerates -> progesterone falls
             -> endometrium breaks down -> next menstruation
 If fertilisation: corpus luteum continues; no menstruation (pregnancy)
```

| Phase | Ovary | Main hormone | Uterus |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Menstrual | Old corpus luteum gone | Low levels | Endometrium shed |
| Follicular | Follicle grows | FSH, oestrogen rising | Endometrium rebuilt |
| Ovulation | Follicle ruptures | **LH surge** | — |
| Luteal | Corpus luteum active | Progesterone (and oestrogen) | Endometrium thick, secretory |

Absence of menstruation can indicate pregnancy, but may also be due to stress, poor health or other causes. Oral contraceptive pills contain synthetic oestrogen and/or progestogen that suppress the LH surge and so prevent ovulation.

## Remember

- Ammonotelic (ammonia, fish), ureotelic (urea, humans), uricotelic (uric acid, birds, reptiles).
- Each kidney has about 1 million nephrons; GFR 125 ml/min = 180 L/day; about 99% reabsorbed; urine 1–1.5 L/day.
- Urine formation = filtration + reabsorption + secretion; most reabsorption in the PCT; ADH acts on DCT and collecting duct.
- Renin (JG cells) → angiotensin I → ACE → angiotensin II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone → BP rises. Renin is not rennin.
- CNS = brain + spinal cord; PNS = 12 pairs cranial + 31 pairs spinal nerves; autonomic = sympathetic + parasympathetic.
- Resting potential about −70 mV; Na+ in = depolarisation; K+ out = repolarisation; Na+/K+ pump 3 out : 2 in; saltatory conduction in myelinated fibres.
- Cerebrum = thinking and voluntary action; cerebellum = balance and coordination; hypothalamus = temperature, hunger, thirst, pituitary control; medulla = breathing and heart.
- Spinal cord: grey matter inside (H-shape), white outside; dorsal root sensory, ventral root motor.
- Insulin lowers, glucagon raises blood glucose; ADH lack = diabetes insipidus; iodine lack = goitre.
- Testes 2–2.5 °C cooler; Sertoli cells nourish, Leydig cells make testosterone.
- 1 primary spermatocyte → 4 sperm; 1 primary oocyte → 1 ovum + polar bodies.
- Cycle 28 days: menstrual 1–5, follicular, ovulation day 14 (LH surge), luteal with corpus luteum and progesterone.

# Unit 4: Plants and mineral nutrition, and photosynthesis

Plants are the source of many drugs (alkaloids, glycosides, volatile oils), and the amount of drug a medicinal plant makes depends on how well it is nourished. This unit explains which mineral elements a plant needs, how it gets nitrogen, and how it makes its own food from light, water and carbon dioxide.

Some words first: **nutrition** is the process of taking in and using food; a **nutrient** is a substance needed for growth and life; an **element** is a basic chemical substance (carbon, nitrogen, iron); **mineral elements** are those a plant takes from the soil as ions (charged particles), as opposed to carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, which come from air and water.

## 4.1 How we know what a plant needs: hydroponics

In 1860 **Julius von Sachs** showed that plants can be grown to maturity in a nutrient solution without soil. Growing plants in a solution of known composition is called **hydroponics**. By leaving out one element at a time and watching whether the plant grows normally, scientists found which elements are essential. Hydroponics is also used commercially to grow tomatoes, seedless cucumbers and lettuce.

```text
   aerating tube (air bubbled in)
        |
   funnel for adding nutrient solution
        |
   [ plant held in cork ]
   [ ~~~ nutrient solution with known mineral salts ~~~ ]
   (roots kept in the dark and aerated)
```

## 4.2 Essential minerals

More than 60 elements are found in plants, but not all are needed. An element is **essential** only if it meets all three **criteria of essentiality**:

1. It must be **absolutely necessary** for normal growth and reproduction; without it the plant cannot complete its life cycle or set seed.
2. The requirement must be **specific**: no other element can replace it.
3. It must be **directly involved** in the plant's metabolism.

On this basis about **17 elements** are essential: carbon (C), hydrogen (H) and oxygen (O) from air and water, and 14 mineral elements from the soil.

### Macro- and micronutrients

| Group | Definition | Elements |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Macronutrients** | Present in large amounts, more than **10 mmol per kg** of dry matter | C, H, O, **N, P, K, S, Ca, Mg** |
| **Micronutrients (trace elements)** | Needed in very small amounts, less than 10 mmol per kg of dry matter | **Fe, Mn, Cu, Mo, Zn, B, Cl, Ni** |

A handy way to remember the micronutrients: "**Mn, Zn, Cu, Mo, B, Cl, Fe, Ni**".

Essential elements can also be grouped by **function**: as parts of body molecules (C, H, O, N); as parts of energy compounds (P in ATP, Mg in chlorophyll); as activators of enzymes (Zn, Mg, Mo); or by changing the osmotic potential of cells (K, which opens and closes stomata).

### Roles and deficiency symptoms

| Element | Absorbed as | Main roles | Deficiency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Nitrogen** | NO3−, NO2−, NH4+ | Needed most; part of proteins, nucleic acids, chlorophyll, vitamins, hormones | Yellowing (chlorosis) starting in older leaves; stunted growth |
| **Phosphorus** | H2PO4−, HPO4^2− | Part of cell membranes, nucleic acids, ATP; needed for phosphorylation reactions | Poor root growth, delayed flowering |
| **Potassium** | K+ | Keeps cation–anion balance; opens and closes stomata; activates enzymes; keeps cells turgid (firm with water) | Chlorosis and dead patches at leaf edges of older leaves |
| **Calcium** | Ca2+ | Forms calcium pectate in the middle lamella of cell walls; spindle formation in cell division | Death (necrosis) of growing tips and young leaves |
| **Magnesium** | Mg2+ | Centre of the **chlorophyll** molecule; activates enzymes of respiration and photosynthesis; holds ribosomes together | Chlorosis between veins of older leaves |
| **Sulphur** | SO4^2− | In amino acids cysteine and methionine, coenzyme A, some vitamins (thiamine, biotin), ferredoxin | Chlorosis of young leaves |
| **Iron** | Fe3+ (mainly) | In ferredoxin and cytochromes (electron carriers); needed to make chlorophyll | Chlorosis of young leaves |
| **Manganese** | Mn2+ | Splitting of water (releasing oxygen) in photosynthesis; activates enzymes | Chlorosis, grey spots |
| **Zinc** | Zn2+ | Activates enzymes (carboxylases); needed to make **auxin** (a growth hormone) | "Little leaf", rosette of small leaves |
| **Copper** | Cu2+ | Redox enzymes; overall metabolism | Necrosis of leaf tips |
| **Boron** | BO3^3−, B4O7^2− | Calcium uptake, pollen germination, cell elongation, carbohydrate movement | Death of shoot tip, poor flowering |
| **Molybdenum** | MoO2^2+ | Part of **nitrogenase** and nitrate reductase (nitrogen metabolism) | Chlorosis, poor nitrogen use |
| **Chlorine** | Cl− | Splitting of water in photosynthesis; solute balance | Wilting |
| **Nickel** | Ni2+ | Part of the enzyme urease | Urea build-up, leaf-tip damage |

### Reading deficiency symptoms

- **Chlorosis** = loss of chlorophyll, leaves turn yellow (N, K, Mg, S, Fe, Mn, Zn, Mo).
- **Necrosis** = death of tissue, especially leaf tissue (Ca, Mg, Cu, K).
- **Mobile elements** (N, K, Mg) are moved from old to new leaves when short, so symptoms appear **first in older leaves**. **Less mobile elements** (S, Ca) stay locked in older tissue, so symptoms appear **first in young leaves and buds**.
- Too much of an element can also harm (**toxicity**). For example, excess manganese hinders the uptake of iron and magnesium, so its toxicity can look like their deficiency.

## 4.3 Nitrogen metabolism

Nitrogen is the element plants need most. Air is about **78% nitrogen gas (N2)**, but plants cannot use N2 directly because the two atoms are held by a very strong triple bond (N≡N). Nitrogen must first be "fixed" into ammonia or nitrate.

**Nitrogen fixation** = conversion of N2 into ammonia (NH3) or other usable compounds. It occurs by:

- **Lightning and ultraviolet radiation** — N2 + O2 → nitrogen oxides (NO, NO2, N2O), which reach the soil with rain.
- **Industrial fixation** — the Haber process makes ammonia for fertilisers.
- **Biological nitrogen fixation** — by living prokaryotes; the most important natural route.

### Nitrogen cycle

```text
              ATMOSPHERIC N2
           /                \
  biological / lightning     \  denitrification
   fixation                    \ (Pseudomonas, Thiobacillus)
        |                       \
        v                        \
   AMMONIA (NH3 / NH4+)      NITRATE (NO3-) in soil
        |   ^                    ^      |
        |   | ammonification     |      | absorbed by roots
        |   | (decay of dead     |      v
        |   |  plants, animals,  |   PLANT PROTEINS -> eaten -> ANIMAL PROTEINS
        |   |  excreta)          |         |                       |
        |   +--------------------|---------+-----------------------+
        |                        | (death, wastes)
        v                        |
  NITRITE (NO2-) ----------------+
  (Nitrosomonas,       nitrification
   Nitrococcus)        (Nitrobacter)
```

| Step | What happens | Organisms |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nitrogen fixation** | N2 → NH3 | Rhizobium, Azotobacter, cyanobacteria, etc. |
| **Ammonification** | Organic nitrogen of dead bodies and wastes → ammonia | Decay bacteria and fungi |
| **Nitrification** step 1 | Ammonia → nitrite (NO2−) | *Nitrosomonas*, *Nitrococcus* |
| **Nitrification** step 2 | Nitrite → nitrate (NO3−) | *Nitrobacter* |
| **Assimilation** | Plants absorb nitrate and ammonium and make amino acids and proteins | Plants |
| **Denitrification** | Nitrate → N2 gas returned to air | *Pseudomonas*, *Thiobacillus* |

Nitrifying bacteria are **chemoautotrophs**: they get energy from oxidising these inorganic compounds.

### Biological nitrogen fixation

Only some prokaryotes can fix nitrogen, because only they have the enzyme **nitrogenase**.

| Type | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Free-living, aerobic | *Azotobacter*, *Beijerinckia* |
| Free-living, anaerobic | *Clostridium*; *Rhodospirillum* (photosynthetic) |
| Cyanobacteria (free-living or symbiotic) | *Anabaena*, *Nostoc* (important in rice fields; *Anabaena* lives in the water fern *Azolla*) |
| **Symbiotic** (living in partnership with a plant) | ***Rhizobium*** in root nodules of **legumes** (pea, gram, groundnut — family Fabaceae); *Frankia* in root nodules of the non-legume *Alnus* |

**Overall reaction (needs a lot of energy):**

```text
 N2 + 8 e- + 8 H+ + 16 ATP  ---nitrogenase--->  2 NH3 + H2 + 16 ADP + 16 Pi
```

### Root nodule formation in legumes

```text
 1. Root releases chemicals; Rhizobium multiplies near the root and
    attaches to root hairs
 2. Root hair curls around the bacteria
 3. Bacteria enter through an INFECTION THREAD that grows into the
    root cortex
 4. Bacteria are released into cortical cells; these cells divide,
    forming a swelling = ROOT NODULE
 5. Bacteria change into nitrogen-fixing forms (bacteroids); the nodule
    gets vascular links with the root for exchange of food and nitrogen
```

- Nitrogenase is **destroyed by oxygen**, so the nodule keeps its inside low in oxygen. It does this with **leghaemoglobin**, a red-pink oxygen-binding pigment (similar to haemoglobin) that gives active nodules their pink colour.
- The plant gives the bacteria sugars and shelter; the bacteria give the plant fixed nitrogen. This is why legumes enrich the soil and are used in **crop rotation**.

### Fate of ammonia in the plant

At the cell's pH, ammonia exists as **ammonium ions (NH4+)**, which are toxic in excess, so they are quickly built into amino acids:

1. **Reductive amination** — ammonia reacts with α-ketoglutaric acid to form the amino acid **glutamic acid**.
2. **Transamination** — the amino group (−NH2) of glutamic acid is transferred to the keto group of other keto acids, making other amino acids. The enzymes are **transaminases**.
3. **Amides** — asparagine and glutamine are formed from amino acids by adding another amino group. They carry more nitrogen and are moved to other parts of the plant in the xylem. In soybean, fixed nitrogen is moved as ureides.

## 4.4 Photosynthesis

### Autotrophic nutrition

**Autotrophs** ("self-feeders") make their own food from inorganic materials. Most use light energy (**photoautotrophs**: green plants, algae, cyanobacteria); a few use chemical energy (**chemoautotrophs**: nitrifying bacteria). **Heterotrophs** depend on autotrophs directly or indirectly. So almost all life on earth depends on photosynthesis for food and for oxygen.

**Photosynthesis** is the process by which green plants use **light energy** absorbed by **chlorophyll** to make **carbohydrates** (glucose) from **carbon dioxide** and **water**, releasing **oxygen**.

```text
                         light energy, chlorophyll
 6 CO2  +  12 H2O  ------------------------------->  C6H12O6  +  6 O2  +  6 H2O
                                                    (glucose)
```

The oxygen released comes from **water**, not from CO2 (shown by van Niel and later with isotopes).

**Site.** Photosynthesis occurs mainly in the **mesophyll** cells of leaves, inside **chloroplasts** (green organelles).

```text
  CHLOROPLAST
  ____________________________________________
 | double membrane                            |
 |   [=][=]  [=][=]   <- GRANA (stacks of     |
 |   [=][=]  [=][=]      thylakoids):         |
 |      \____/           LIGHT REACTION       |
 |   stroma lamellae                          |
 |   ~~~ STROMA (fluid with enzymes,          |
 |       DNA, ribosomes): DARK REACTION ~~~   |
 |____________________________________________|
```

### Photosynthetic pigments

**Pigments** are substances that absorb light of particular wavelengths. They can be separated by **paper chromatography**.

| Pigment | Colour | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Chlorophyll a** | Bright or blue-green | **Chief pigment**; forms the reaction centres of the photosystems |
| Chlorophyll b | Yellow-green | Accessory pigment |
| Xanthophylls | Yellow | Accessory pigment |
| Carotenoids (carotenes) | Yellow to yellow-orange | Accessory pigments; also protect chlorophyll from damage by strong light (photo-oxidation) |

- Chlorophyll absorbs mostly **blue and red light**; green light is reflected, which is why leaves look green.
- **Accessory pigments** absorb other wavelengths and pass the energy on to chlorophyll a, widening the range of light that can be used.
- An **absorption spectrum** shows how much light a pigment absorbs at each wavelength; an **action spectrum** shows the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength. They match closely, proving chlorophyll does the work.

### Stages of photosynthesis

| | Light reaction (photochemical phase) | Dark reaction (biosynthetic phase, Calvin cycle) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where | Thylakoid membranes of grana | Stroma |
| Needs light directly | Yes | No (but depends on products of the light reaction) |
| Inputs | Light, water, ADP, NADP+ | CO2, ATP, NADPH |
| Outputs | **ATP, NADPH**, O2 | **Sugar** (glucose), ADP, NADP+ |

**Light reaction**

1. **Light absorption** by pigments grouped into two **photosystems**: **PS I** (reaction centre chlorophyll a absorbing at **700 nm**, called **P700**) and **PS II** (reaction centre **P680**).
2. **Splitting of water (photolysis)** at PS II: 2H2O → 4H+ + O2 + 4e−. This gives electrons to PS II and releases oxygen. Manganese and chlorine help here.
3. **Electron transport:** excited electrons pass from PS II along carriers (an electron transport chain) to PS I and then to **NADP+**, reducing it to **NADPH**. Drawn on an energy scale, the path looks like the letter Z, so it is called the **Z-scheme**.
4. **Photophosphorylation** — making ATP using light energy:
   - **Non-cyclic**: both photosystems, electrons do not return; produces **ATP + NADPH + O2**.
   - **Cyclic**: only PS I; electrons return to PS I; produces **ATP only** (no NADPH, no O2); occurs in stroma lamellae.
5. ATP is made by **chemiosmosis**: H+ ions build up inside the thylakoid and flow back out through the enzyme **ATP synthase**, which uses this flow to make ATP.

**Dark reaction — Calvin cycle (C3 pathway)**

Worked out by **Melvin Calvin** using radioactive carbon (14C). The first stable product is a **3-carbon** compound, **3-phosphoglyceric acid (PGA)**, so plants using only this route are called **C3 plants** (wheat, rice, most plants).

```text
 1. CARBOXYLATION: CO2 + RuBP (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate, 5 carbon)
       --RuBisCO--> 2 molecules of 3-PGA
 2. REDUCTION: 3-PGA --(ATP, NADPH)--> glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (a sugar);
       some leaves the cycle to make glucose and starch
 3. REGENERATION: the rest is used to remake RuBP (uses ATP), so the cycle
       continues
```

- **RuBisCO** (RuBP carboxylase–oxygenase) is the **most abundant enzyme on earth**.
- To make **one glucose** molecule, 6 turns of the cycle are needed, using **18 ATP and 12 NADPH**.

**C4 pathway (Hatch and Slack pathway)** — in plants of hot, dry tropical regions such as **maize, sugarcane and sorghum** (Poaceae):

- The first CO2 acceptor is **PEP (phosphoenolpyruvate)**, and the first stable product is a **4-carbon** compound, **oxaloacetic acid (OAA)**, made by **PEP carboxylase** in mesophyll cells.
- The 4-carbon acid moves to **bundle sheath cells** around the veins, releases CO2 there, and the Calvin cycle runs in those cells.
- C4 leaves show **Kranz anatomy** ("wreath"): large bundle sheath cells in a ring around each vein.
- C4 plants avoid **photorespiration** (a wasteful process in C3 plants in which RuBisCO binds O2 instead of CO2, losing fixed carbon), so they make more sugar in heat and strong light.

### Factors affecting photosynthesis

**Blackman's law of limiting factors (1905):** if a chemical process depends on several factors, its rate is controlled by the factor that is nearest to its minimum value; changing that factor changes the rate.

```text
 rate of photosynthesis
   |            ________  (limited by CO2 here)
   |          /
   |        /
   |      /   (limited by light here)
   |    /
   |__/_____________________ light intensity
```

| Factor | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| **Light** | Rate rises with light intensity at low levels; at high intensity other factors limit it; very strong light can damage chlorophyll. Quality (wavelength) and duration also matter |
| **Carbon dioxide** | Major limiting factor because air has only about 0.03–0.04% CO2; raising it increases the rate (used in greenhouses for tomatoes and bell peppers); C4 plants saturate at lower CO2 levels than C3 plants |
| **Temperature** | Dark reactions are enzyme-controlled, so the rate rises with temperature up to an optimum and then falls; C4 plants have higher optima than C3 plants |
| **Water** | Shortage closes stomata (less CO2 enters) and makes leaves wilt; affects the plant more through these effects than as a direct raw material |
| Internal factors | Number, size and age of leaves, amount of chlorophyll, leaf orientation, CO2 concentration inside the leaf |

## Remember

- Hydroponics (von Sachs, 1860) identifies essential elements.
- Criteria: absolutely necessary, specific (not replaceable), directly involved in metabolism.
- Macronutrients (>10 mmol/kg dry matter): C, H, O, N, P, K, S, Ca, Mg. Micronutrients: Fe, Mn, Cu, Mo, Zn, B, Cl, Ni.
- Mg is in chlorophyll; Mo in nitrogenase; Zn for auxin; Mn and Cl for splitting water; K for stomata.
- Mobile elements (N, K, Mg): symptoms in older leaves; immobile (S, Ca): in young leaves.
- Nitrification: NH3 → NO2− (*Nitrosomonas*) → NO3− (*Nitrobacter*); denitrification: *Pseudomonas*, *Thiobacillus*.
- Nitrogenase needs anaerobic conditions; leghaemoglobin protects it in nodules; N2 fixation costs 16 ATP per N2.
- Ammonia → glutamic acid (reductive amination) → other amino acids (transamination); amides asparagine and glutamine.
- 6CO2 + 12H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2 + 6H2O; O2 comes from water.
- Chlorophyll a is the chief pigment; absorbs blue and red; PS I = P700, PS II = P680.
- Light reaction (grana) gives ATP, NADPH, O2; Calvin cycle (stroma) uses 18 ATP + 12 NADPH per glucose; RuBisCO fixes CO2 into 3-PGA.
- C4 plants (maize, sugarcane): PEP carboxylase, OAA, Kranz anatomy, no photorespiration.
- Blackman: the factor in shortest supply limits the rate.

# Unit 5: Plant respiration, plant growth and development, the cell and tissues

This unit closes the course with the smallest units of life. First it shows how plants release energy from food (respiration) and how they grow under the control of hormones. Then it looks inside the cell, explains how cells divide, and describes the tissues that cells form in plants and animals. Fermentation, plant hormones and cell division are directly useful later: fermentation makes ethanol and antibiotics, synthetic plant hormones are used in farming, and many anticancer drugs act on dividing cells.

## 5.1 Plant respiration

**Respiration** is the breakdown of food molecules (mainly glucose) inside cells, with release of energy that is trapped as **ATP (adenosine triphosphate)**, the cell's "energy currency". The compounds broken down are called **respiratory substrates** (carbohydrates usually; fats and proteins in some conditions).

```text
 C6H12O6 + 6 O2  --->  6 CO2 + 6 H2O + energy (stored as ATP, part lost as heat)
```

Plants have no special breathing organs. Each part takes in and gives out gases by itself, through **stomata** (pores in leaves) and **lenticels** (pores in bark). Plants need relatively little oxygen because most of their cells are near the surface and their energy demand is lower than that of animals.

**Aerobic respiration** uses oxygen and completely breaks glucose to CO2 and water. **Anaerobic respiration (fermentation)** occurs without oxygen and breaks glucose only partly. Both begin with **glycolysis**.

### Glycolysis (EMP pathway)

**Glycolysis** ("splitting of sugar") is the breakdown of one glucose (6 carbons) into **two pyruvic acid** (3 carbons each) molecules. It was worked out by Gustav Embden, Otto Meyerhof and J. Parnas, so it is also called the **EMP pathway**. It takes place in the **cytoplasm**, does not need oxygen, and occurs in all living organisms.

```text
 Glucose (6C)
   | ATP -> ADP   (hexokinase)
 Glucose-6-phosphate
   |
 Fructose-6-phosphate
   | ATP -> ADP   (phosphofructokinase)
 Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (6C)
   |  split (aldolase)
 2 x triose phosphate (3C): glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (and DHAP, converted to it)
   |  2 NAD+ -> 2 NADH  (oxidation + phosphate added)
 2 x 1,3-bisphosphoglyceric acid
   |  2 ADP -> 2 ATP
 2 x 3-phosphoglyceric acid
   |
 2 x 2-phosphoglyceric acid
   |  (water removed)
 2 x phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP)
   |  2 ADP -> 2 ATP
 2 x PYRUVIC ACID (3C)
```

**Energy account of glycolysis (per glucose)**

| Item | Number |
| --- | --- |
| ATP used | 2 |
| ATP formed | 4 |
| **Net ATP** | **2** |
| NADH formed | 2 |

In plants, glucose for glycolysis comes from sucrose (split by invertase into glucose and fructose) or from stored starch.

**Fate of pyruvic acid** depends on the cell's needs and on oxygen:

```text
                     PYRUVIC ACID
          ______________|______________________
         |                  |                  |
  no O2 (yeast,      no O2 (some        O2 present (most plant
  some plants)        bacteria, muscle)  and animal cells)
         |                  |                  |
  ethanol + CO2       lactic acid        Krebs cycle in mitochondria
  (alcoholic          (lactic acid       -> CO2 + H2O + much ATP
   fermentation)       fermentation)      (aerobic respiration)
```

### Fermentation (anaerobic respiration)

**Fermentation** is the incomplete breakdown of glucose in the absence of oxygen, giving ethanol or lactic acid plus a little energy.

**Alcoholic fermentation** (yeast, *Saccharomyces cerevisiae*):

```text
 Pyruvic acid --pyruvic acid decarboxylase--> Acetaldehyde + CO2
 Acetaldehyde + NADH --alcohol dehydrogenase--> Ethanol + NAD+

 Overall: C6H12O6 ---> 2 C2H5OH + 2 CO2 + energy (net 2 ATP)
```

**Lactic acid fermentation** (lactic acid bacteria such as *Lactobacillus*; animal muscle during hard exercise when oxygen runs short):

```text
 Pyruvic acid + NADH --lactate dehydrogenase--> Lactic acid + NAD+
```

**Key points**

- The NADH made in glycolysis is reused (turned back to NAD+) in fermentation, so glycolysis can keep going.
- Less than **7%** of the energy in glucose is released, and not all of it as ATP.
- Yeasts are poisoned and die when ethanol reaches about **13%**, which sets the upper alcohol content of naturally fermented drinks; higher strengths need distillation.
- Uses: bread (CO2 makes dough rise), alcoholic drinks and industrial alcohol, curd (lactic acid), vinegar, many antibiotics and vitamins are made by fermentation processes.

### Aerobic respiration (for completeness)

In mitochondria, pyruvic acid is converted to **acetyl CoA** (releasing CO2 and NADH), which enters the **Krebs cycle (citric acid / TCA cycle)**. The NADH and FADH2 formed pass electrons along the **electron transport system** in the inner mitochondrial membrane to **oxygen**, which is the final electron acceptor and forms water. ATP is made by **oxidative phosphorylation**. Complete oxidation of one glucose gives a net of about **38 ATP** in the classical textbook count (current estimates are lower, about 30–32).

| Aerobic respiration | Anaerobic respiration (fermentation) |
| --- | --- |
| Needs oxygen | No oxygen |
| Cytoplasm + mitochondria | Cytoplasm only |
| Glucose fully broken to CO2 and H2O | Partial breakdown to ethanol + CO2 or lactic acid |
| Large energy yield (about 38 ATP) | Small energy yield (2 ATP) |

### Respiratory quotient (RQ)

**RQ = volume of CO2 released ÷ volume of O2 used** in respiration.

| Substrate | RQ |
| --- | --- |
| Carbohydrates | 1.0 |
| Fats (e.g. tripalmitin) | Less than 1 (about 0.7) |
| Proteins | About 0.9 |
| Organic acids | More than 1 |
| Anaerobic respiration | Very high (CO2 released, no O2 used) |

## 5.2 Plant growth and development

**Growth** is a permanent, irreversible increase in the size, mass or volume of an organism or its part, usually with an increase in dry weight and in the number of cells.

- Plant growth is **indeterminate (open)**: plants keep growing throughout life because they have **meristems** (regions of dividing cells) at root and shoot tips and in the stem's sides.
- **Primary growth** (increase in length) comes from **apical meristems** at root and shoot tips; **secondary growth** (increase in thickness) from **lateral meristems** (vascular cambium and cork cambium) in dicots and gymnosperms.
- **Development** is the whole series of changes an organism goes through from seed germination to old age and death; it includes growth and **differentiation**.

### Phases of growth

```text
  Root or shoot tip:
  [ MERISTEMATIC ] -> [ ELONGATION ] -> [ MATURATION ]
  constantly dividing  cells enlarge,     cells reach full size,
  cells, dense          large vacuole,     thicker walls,
  cytoplasm, large      new wall material  change in structure
  nucleus, thin walls                      (differentiation)
```

### Rate of plant growth

**Growth rate** is the increase in growth per unit time.

| Type | Pattern | Formula |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Arithmetic growth** | After mitosis only one daughter cell keeps dividing; the other differentiates. Length increases at a constant rate | Lt = L0 + rt (Lt = length at time t, L0 at start, r = growth rate). Graph is a straight line |
| **Geometric (exponential) growth** | Both daughter cells keep dividing; growth is slow at first, then rapid | W1 = W0 e^(rt) (W = size, r = relative growth rate, e = base of natural logarithms) |

When cells, tissues or a whole organism grow geometrically with limited resources, growth slows down and the graph is **S-shaped (sigmoid)**:

```text
 size
   |                 ________ stationary (steady) phase
   |               /
   |             /   log (exponential) phase - fastest growth
   |           /
   |   ______/  lag phase - slow start
   |__________________________ time
```

**Absolute growth rate** = total growth per unit time; **relative growth rate** = growth per unit time per unit of initial size. Two leaves may grow by the same absolute amount, but the smaller one has the higher relative growth rate.

### Conditions for growth

| Condition | Why it is needed |
| --- | --- |
| **Water** | Cell enlargement needs turgidity (cells filled with water); medium for enzyme reactions |
| **Oxygen** | Respiration to release energy for growth |
| **Nutrients** | Macro- and micronutrients to build protoplasm and as energy sources |
| **Optimum temperature** | Enzymes work within a range; extremes damage or stop growth |
| **Light and gravity** | Influence some stages and the direction of growth (tropisms) |

### Differentiation, dedifferentiation, redifferentiation

- **Differentiation** — cells from meristems become specialised for particular jobs (for example, xylem cells lose their protoplasm and build strong walls for water transport).
- **Dedifferentiation** — permanent cells regain the ability to divide (for example, formation of cork cambium from mature parenchyma).
- **Redifferentiation** — cells formed by dedifferentiated tissue specialise again (for example, cork cells).
- **Plasticity** — a plant forms different structures in response to the environment or life stage. Example: **heterophylly**, different leaf shapes in young and mature plants of cotton, coriander and larkspur, or above-water and under-water leaves of buttercup.

### Introduction to plant growth regulators

**Plant growth regulators (PGRs)**, also called plant hormones or phytohormones, are small organic substances that, in tiny amounts, control growth and development. Some are **promoters** (auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins) and some mainly **inhibitors** (abscisic acid); ethylene does both but is largely an inhibitor.

| PGR | Discovery (short) | Main physiological effects | Uses |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Auxins** — natural: indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), indole butyric acid (IBA); synthetic: NAA, 2,4-D | Charles and Francis Darwin noticed coleoptiles of canary grass bend towards light; F. W. Went isolated auxin from oat (*Avena*) coleoptile tips | Cell elongation; **apical dominance** (the growing tip suppresses side buds); root formation on stem cuttings; xylem differentiation | Rooting of cuttings; prevent early fruit and leaf drop; **parthenocarpy** (seedless fruits, e.g. tomato); 2,4-D kills broad-leaved (dicot) weeds in cereal crops |
| **Gibberellins** (more than 100 kinds; GA3 studied most) | E. Kurosawa found that the fungus *Gibberella fujikuroi* caused "foolish seedling" (bakanae) disease of rice, in which seedlings grow abnormally tall | Stem elongation; **bolting** (sudden stem growth before flowering) in cabbage and beet; break seed dormancy | Increase length of grape stalks; longer sugarcane stems (more sugar); speed up malting in brewing |
| **Cytokinins** — kinetin (from heated DNA), natural zeatin (from maize kernels, coconut milk) | F. Skoog and co-workers found a substance promoting cell division | **Cell division (cytokinesis)**; new leaves and shoots; overcome apical dominance; **delay leaf senescence** (ageing) | Keep cut flowers and vegetables fresh longer; tissue culture |
| **Abscisic acid (ABA)** | Identified as a growth inhibitor linked with leaf and fruit fall and dormancy | **Stress hormone**; closes stomata in drought; induces seed and bud **dormancy**; inhibits germination; aids seed maturation | — |
| **Ethylene** (a simple gas, C2H4) | H. H. Cousins found that ripe oranges released a gas that ripened stored bananas | **Fruit ripening** (raises respiration rate: climacteric); abscission (fall) of leaves and flowers; breaks dormancy; promotes female flowers in cucumber | **Ethephon** releases ethylene: ripening of fruits like tomato and apple, flowering in pineapple |

Plant growth and development also depend on day length (**photoperiodism**) and on cold treatment (**vernalisation**), which the syllabus does not cover in detail.

## 5.3 The cell — the unit of life

A **cell** is the smallest structural and functional unit of life. Robert Hooke first saw "cells" in cork (1665); Anton van Leeuwenhoek first saw living cells.

**Cell theory**

1. All living organisms are made of cells and cell products (Schleiden, for plants, 1838; Schwann, for animals, 1839).
2. All cells arise from pre-existing cells — "*omnis cellula e cellula*" (Rudolf Virchow, 1855).

### Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells

| Feature | Prokaryotic cell | Eukaryotic cell |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Examples | Bacteria, cyanobacteria, mycoplasma | Protists, fungi, plants, animals |
| Nucleus | No true nucleus; DNA lies in the cytoplasm as the **nucleoid** | True nucleus with nuclear envelope |
| Membrane-bound organelles | Absent | Present (mitochondria, ER, Golgi, plastids) |
| Ribosomes | 70S | 80S in cytoplasm (70S inside mitochondria and chloroplasts) |
| Size | Small, about 1–10 µm | Larger, about 10–100 µm |
| Extra DNA | Often **plasmids** (small circular DNA; can carry antibiotic resistance) | Not usual |

### Plant cell and animal cell

```text
   PLANT CELL                             ANIMAL CELL
   ____________________________           ______________________
  | cell wall (cellulose)       |        ( plasma membrane only  )
  | plasma membrane             |        (    nucleus            )
  |   [ large central vacuole ] |        (  small vacuoles       )
  |   nucleus     chloroplasts  |        (  centrioles (centrosome)
  |   mitochondria  Golgi  ER   |        (  mitochondria Golgi ER)
  |_____________________________|        (  lysosomes            )
```

| Feature | Plant cell | Animal cell |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cell wall | Present (cellulose) | Absent |
| Plastids (chloroplasts) | Present | Absent |
| Vacuole | One large central vacuole | Small, few or absent |
| Centrioles | Absent (in higher plants) | Present |
| Shape | Usually regular, rectangular | Usually rounded or irregular |
| Stored food | Starch | Glycogen |

### Structure and functions of cell organelles

| Structure | Structure in short | Function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Cell wall** | Non-living rigid layer of plant cells: cellulose, hemicellulose, pectin; primary wall, secondary wall; neighbouring cells joined by the **middle lamella** (calcium pectate); **plasmodesmata** connect cells | Shape, protection, support; prevents bursting |
| **Plasma (cell) membrane** | **Fluid mosaic model** (Singer and Nicolson, 1972): a **lipid bilayer** (phospholipids, tails inward) with proteins scattered in it, some on the surface, some passing through; the lipids and proteins can move sideways | Controls what enters and leaves (**selectively permeable**); passive transport (diffusion, osmosis) and active transport using ATP (e.g. Na+/K+ pump) |
| **Nucleus** | Bounded by a double **nuclear envelope** with pores; contains **nucleoplasm**, **chromatin** (DNA + proteins, forms chromosomes during division) and one or more **nucleoli** | Controls all cell activity; stores hereditary information; nucleolus makes ribosomal RNA |
| **Endoplasmic reticulum (ER)** | Network of membrane tubes and sacs. **Rough ER** has ribosomes on its surface; **smooth ER** has none | Rough ER: protein synthesis and secretion. Smooth ER: lipid and steroid synthesis; detoxification of drugs (in liver cells) |
| **Golgi apparatus** | Stacks of flat sacs (cisternae) with a receiving (cis) and a shipping (trans) face | Packages and modifies proteins (adds sugars: glycoproteins), forms secretory vesicles and lysosomes |
| **Lysosomes** | Membrane sacs with **hydrolytic (digestive) enzymes** that work at acidic pH | Digest worn-out organelles and engulfed particles; "suicide bags" because they can digest the cell itself |
| **Vacuoles** | Membrane-bound spaces; in plants a large central vacuole bounded by the **tonoplast** | Store water, sap, wastes; keep the plant cell turgid |
| **Mitochondria** | Double membrane; inner membrane folded into **cristae**; inner space (**matrix**) has its own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes | "**Powerhouse of the cell**": aerobic respiration, ATP formation |
| **Plastids** | In plants. **Chloroplasts** (green, double membrane, grana and stroma, own DNA), **chromoplasts** (coloured carotenoids in fruits and petals), **leucoplasts** (colourless stores: amyloplasts for starch, elaioplasts for oil, aleuroplasts for protein) | Photosynthesis; colour; storage |
| **Ribosomes** | Non-membrane granules of RNA and protein; 80S (60S + 40S) in eukaryotes, 70S (50S + 30S) in prokaryotes | **Protein synthesis** |
| **Cytoskeleton** | Network of microtubules, microfilaments and intermediate filaments | Support, shape, movement of the cell and organelles |
| **Cilia and flagella** | Hair-like outgrowths; core (axoneme) of microtubules in a **9 + 2** pattern | Movement of the cell or of fluid over it |
| **Centrosome** | Two **centrioles** at right angles, each with nine triplets of microtubules (9 + 0) | Forms spindle fibres in animal cell division; base of cilia and flagella |
| **Microbodies** | Small vesicles with enzymes (peroxisomes, glyoxysomes) | Various reactions, e.g. breaking down hydrogen peroxide |

### Cell division

**Cell division** is how one cell becomes two. It allows growth, repair and reproduction.

**Cell cycle** — the sequence of events from one division to the next (about 24 hours in a human cell in culture):

```text
          INTERPHASE (about 95% of the time)
   G1 phase -----> S phase -----> G2 phase -----> M phase (division)
 (cell grows,    (DNA is copied,  (proteins made   mitosis + cytokinesis
  normal work)    doubled)         for division)        |
       ^________________________________________________|
 Cells that stop dividing leave G1 and enter G0 (quiescent stage).
```

### Mitosis (equational division)

In mitosis one cell divides into **two identical daughter cells**, each with the **same chromosome number** as the parent (2n → 2n). It happens in body (somatic) cells; in plants mainly in meristems.

| Stage | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| **Prophase** | Chromatin condenses into visible **chromosomes**, each with two **chromatids** joined at the **centromere**; centrioles move to opposite poles and form spindle fibres (animal cells); nucleolus and nuclear envelope disappear |
| **Metaphase** | Chromosomes line up at the cell's equator (**metaphase plate**); spindle fibres attach to the **kinetochores** at the centromeres. Best stage to count and study chromosomes |
| **Anaphase** | Centromeres split; sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles |
| **Telophase** | Chromosomes reach the poles and uncoil; nuclear envelope and nucleolus re-form; two nuclei |
| **Cytokinesis** | Cytoplasm divides: in animal cells by a **furrow** that pinches in; in plant cells by a **cell plate** formed from the centre outwards |

**Significance:** growth, repair and replacement of cells; keeps the chromosome number constant; asexual reproduction. Uncontrolled mitosis produces **cancer**.

### Meiosis (reductional division)

Meiosis occurs in cells that form **gametes** (or spores in plants). One diploid cell divides **twice** to give **four haploid cells** (2n → n), which are genetically different.

```text
 Diploid cell (2n)
      |  MEIOSIS I (reductional): homologous chromosomes pair and separate
      v
 2 haploid cells (n), chromosomes still double (two chromatids each)
      |  MEIOSIS II (like mitosis): sister chromatids separate
      v
 4 haploid cells (n)
```

**Prophase I** is long and has five substages:

| Substage | Event |
| --- | --- |
| Leptotene | Chromosomes become visible as long threads |
| Zygotene | **Homologous chromosomes** (matching pairs, one from each parent) pair up (**synapsis**), forming **bivalents** |
| Pachytene | **Crossing over** — exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids of homologues (enzyme recombinase) |
| Diplotene | Homologues begin to separate but stay joined at the cross-over points (**chiasmata**) |
| Diakinesis | Chiasmata move to the ends; spindle forms; nuclear envelope and nucleolus disappear |

Then **metaphase I** (bivalents line up), **anaphase I** (homologous chromosomes, not chromatids, move apart), **telophase I**; a short gap (interkinesis, no DNA copying) and **meiosis II** (prophase II to telophase II).

| Mitosis | Meiosis |
| --- | --- |
| Body (somatic) cells | Reproductive cells (gamete or spore formation) |
| One division | Two divisions |
| 2 daughter cells | 4 daughter cells |
| Chromosome number stays the same (2n → 2n) | Halved (2n → n) |
| No pairing, no crossing over | Pairing and crossing over in prophase I |
| Daughter cells identical | Daughter cells genetically different |

**Significance of meiosis:** keeps the chromosome number constant from generation to generation (fertilisation restores 2n); crossing over and random sorting of chromosomes create **variation**, the raw material of evolution.

## 5.4 Tissues

A **tissue** is a group of cells, usually of similar structure and common origin, working together for a particular function. **Histology** is the study of tissues.

### Plant tissues

```text
                   PLANT TISSUES
          ________________|________________
         |                                 |
   MERISTEMATIC (dividing)           PERMANENT (no longer dividing)
   apical, intercalary, lateral      _________|__________
                                    |                    |
                              SIMPLE (one type     COMPLEX (several
                              of cell)             types of cell)
                              parenchyma           xylem
                              collenchyma          phloem
                              sclerenchyma
```

| Tissue | Location | Features | Function |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Apical meristem** | Tips of root and shoot | Small, dividing cells | Growth in length (primary growth) |
| **Intercalary meristem** | Base of internodes or leaves of grasses | Dividing cells between mature tissue | Regrowth of grazed grasses; elongation |
| **Lateral meristem** | Sides of stems and roots (vascular cambium, cork cambium) | Dividing cells in a cylinder | Growth in thickness (secondary growth) |
| **Parenchyma** | Cortex, pith, mesophyll, fruit pulp | Living, thin-walled, cellulose walls, spaces between cells | Storage, photosynthesis (as chlorenchyma), secretion |
| **Collenchyma** | Below epidermis of dicot stems, petioles | Living; walls thickened at the corners with cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin | Mechanical support to growing parts; flexibility |
| **Sclerenchyma** | Hypodermis of monocot stems, fruit walls, seed coats, around vascular bundles | Dead at maturity; thick walls with **lignin**; **fibres** (long) and **sclereids** (short, stony cells in nut shells, guava pulp, pear) | Strength and rigidity |
| **Xylem** | Vascular bundles | **Tracheids** and **vessels** (dead, lignified, conduct water), **xylem fibres** (support), **xylem parenchyma** (living, store food) | Conducts water and minerals upward from roots; support |
| **Phloem** | Vascular bundles | **Sieve tube elements** (living, no nucleus, sieve plates), **companion cells** (control sieve tubes), **phloem parenchyma**, **phloem fibres** (bast) | Conducts food (sugars) from leaves to other parts |

Vessels are the main water-conducting cells of angiosperms; gymnosperms have mainly tracheids. Companion cells are typical of angiosperms.

### Animal tissues

There are four basic animal tissues.

**1. Epithelial tissue** — covers the body surface and lines cavities, ducts and tubes. Cells are packed closely with very little space between them, resting on a **basement membrane**.

| Type | Structure | Location | Function |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Squamous** (simple) | One layer of flat cells | Walls of blood vessels, air sacs (alveoli) of lungs | Diffusion, filtration |
| **Cuboidal** (simple) | One layer of cube-shaped cells | Ducts of glands, tubular parts of nephrons | Secretion, absorption |
| **Columnar** (simple) | One layer of tall cells, often with **microvilli** | Lining of stomach and intestine | Secretion, absorption |
| **Ciliated** | Cuboidal or columnar with cilia | Bronchioles, fallopian tubes | Move mucus or eggs along |
| **Compound (stratified)** | Several layers | Skin, lining of mouth and pharynx, inner lining of salivary and pancreatic ducts | Protection against chemical and mechanical stress |
| **Glandular** | Cells specialised for secretion | Exocrine glands (salivary, sweat) and endocrine glands | Secretion |

Cells are linked by **junctions**: **tight junctions** stop leakage, **adhering junctions** cement cells, **gap junctions** let ions and small molecules pass between cells.

**2. Connective tissue** — the most abundant and widely spread tissue; links and supports other tissues. Cells lie scattered in a **matrix** (ground substance) with fibres such as **collagen** and **elastin**.

| Type | Structure | Location | Function |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Loose — areolar** | Fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells, loose fibres | Beneath the skin | Packing, supports epithelium |
| **Loose — adipose** | Fat-storing cells | Under the skin, around kidneys | Stores fat, insulation, cushioning |
| **Dense regular** | Collagen fibres in parallel bundles | **Tendons** (muscle to bone), **ligaments** (bone to bone) | Strong attachment |
| **Dense irregular** | Fibres in many directions | Skin (dermis) | Strength in many directions |
| **Cartilage** | Solid, pliable matrix; cells (chondrocytes) in small cavities | Tip of nose, outer ear, ends of long bones, between vertebrae | Support with flexibility |
| **Bone** | Hard matrix rich in **calcium salts** and collagen; cells (osteocytes) in spaces called lacunae | Skeleton | Support, protection, movement; bone marrow forms blood cells |
| **Blood** | Fluid matrix (plasma) with RBC, WBC, platelets | Blood vessels | Transport (see Unit 2) |

**3. Muscular tissue** — made of long cells called **muscle fibres** that contain contractile filaments (actin and myosin) and can contract.

| Type | Features | Location | Control |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Skeletal (striated)** | Long, cylindrical, unbranched, many nuclei, cross stripes | Attached to bones (e.g. biceps) | Voluntary |
| **Smooth (unstriated)** | Spindle-shaped, one nucleus, no stripes | Walls of stomach, intestine, blood vessels, uterus | Involuntary |
| **Cardiac** | Branched, striated, usually one nucleus; joined by **intercalated discs** (gap junctions) so the heart contracts as a unit | Heart wall | Involuntary |

**4. Neural (nervous) tissue** — **neurons** (excitable cells that carry impulses, see Unit 3) and **neuroglia** (supporting cells that protect and support neurons and make up more than half the volume of neural tissue). Found in brain, spinal cord and nerves. Function: control and coordination.

## Remember

- Glycolysis: cytoplasm, no O2, glucose → 2 pyruvic acid, net 2 ATP + 2 NADH.
- Yeast: pyruvic acid → acetaldehyde + CO2 → ethanol (decarboxylase, alcohol dehydrogenase); muscle and *Lactobacillus*: lactic acid. Yeast dies at about 13% alcohol.
- RQ = CO2 released/O2 used: carbohydrate 1, fat about 0.7, protein about 0.9.
- Growth phases: meristematic → elongation → maturation; sigmoid curve: lag, log, stationary.
- Arithmetic Lt = L0 + rt; geometric W1 = W0 e^rt.
- Auxin: apical dominance, rooting, 2,4-D weedkiller; gibberellin: bolting, malting, sugarcane; cytokinin: cell division, delays senescence; ABA: stress, dormancy, stomata close; ethylene: ripening.
- Cell theory: Schleiden, Schwann; *omnis cellula e cellula* — Virchow.
- Fluid mosaic model: Singer and Nicolson (1972). Mitochondria = powerhouse; lysosomes = suicide bags; ribosomes 70S/80S.
- Mitosis: 2n → 2n, 2 identical cells, PMAT; meiosis: 2n → n, 4 different cells, crossing over in pachytene.
- Plant tissues: meristematic and permanent (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma; xylem, phloem).
- Animal tissues: epithelial, connective, muscular, neural; tendons join muscle to bone, ligaments bone to bone.
